name: A lo Cortico
summary: A musicality and styling Rueda call where couples shrink their step size to ultra-compact, grounded micro-steps in closed or close hold to match a quiet or breakdown section of the song, without changing partners.

leaderSteps.text: Transition into closed social hold (or compact Guapea) and compress the step size to tiny, grounded transfers directly underneath the hips on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, softening the frame.
Continue the compact groove with subtle Cuban hip and ribcage isolation on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), then open out or lead a gentle Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) when the caller releases the call.

followerSteps.text: Match the leader's lowered energy and close proximity by taking miniature steps directly underneath the body on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, maintaining a light, responsive frame.
Maintain the small, rhythmic footwork on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and expand smoothly back to normal stride length during the Dile Que No exit on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Stopping the feet completely instead of keeping the 1-2-3, 5-6-7 weight transfers alive underneath the hips.
Hunching the shoulders forward when making the steps smaller.
Continuing to take wide Guapea rock steps that break the unified visual effect of the Rueda.
variations: Enchufla a lo cortico (doing tiny half-turns in close proximity without full arm extensions).
notes: UNSURE: Some schools use 'A lo cortico' as a continuous groove modifier (like 'por el piso' or 'chiquitico'), while others use it for a specific clipped Enchufla check on counts 1-3 and 5-7. Verify which version your curriculum teaches.

name: Abajo y Arriba (Closed-Position Basic)
summary: The foundational rotating closed-position Casino basic: 'Arriba' rotates clockwise around the couple's shared axis, while 'Abajo' reverses or steps back-and-side to travel anticlockwise.

leaderSteps.text: In closed hold, step left foot forward/across to rotate clockwise (Arriba) on 1, transfer weight in place on right on 2, and bring left foot together on 3.
Step right foot back/behind on 5, rock onto left foot on 6, and close right foot on 7 while maintaining continuous circular rotation.
To transition to Abajo, soften the right shoulder lead and step left foot slightly back/open on 9-11 and right foot back on 13-15, guiding the closed couple in the opposite rotational feel.

followerSteps.text: In closed hold, step right foot back on 1, rock onto left foot on 2, and close right foot on 3 while matching the leader's clockwise torso rotation.
Step left foot forward between/around the leader's stance on 5, pivot slightly on 6, and close left foot on 7.
Follow the leader's chest frame shift into Abajo by taking compact back-open steps on 9-11 and 13-15 without letting your hips drift away from the shared center.

commonMistakes: Bouncing vertically with the shoulders instead of keeping knees soft and grounded.
Taking huge steps that break the compact closed embrace.
Leading the direction change with the hands rather than the ribcage and right scapula connection.
variations: Adding a pause/freeze on 4 and 8 with subtle Cuban hip pendulum.
notes: In Rueda de Casino, 'Vamos Arriba' and 'Vamos Abajo' also refer to marching forward or backing up around the circle; in partnerwork, it refers to the closed-hold rotational basic.

name: Abanico
summary: The 'Fan': an elegant, sweeping Casino figure where the leader fans the follower across and around the circle with continuous rotational momentum and overhead arm work.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an initial turn entry on 1-3 and sweep the follower across your front in a wide fan-like arc on 5-7.
Check the circular momentum gently on 1-3 and guide the follower back around the opposite arc on 5-7 with a fluid overhead pass.
Collect the follower in open/semi-closed frame on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn cleanly on 1-3 and travel along the wide circular fan arc on 5-7 with poised posture and active core balance.
Feel the direction check on 3, pivot smoothly, and glide along the return arc on 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: Letting the wide fan arc pull the couple off balance; keep steps underneath your hips.
Leading the direction check with a harsh arm yank instead of a gradual torso absorb on count 3.
Dropping the elbow during the overhead pass.
variations: Abanico Complicado (adding a double follower spin on the fan exit).
notes: UNSURE: 'El Abanico' has two common syllabus versions (one based on a Setenta/Sombrero knot, another based on a sweeping fan walk). Teacher should confirm BOH Studios' version.

name: Abanico y Cadeneta
summary: A Rueda combination that opens with the circular Abanico figure and flows directly into a travelling Cadeneta chain around the circle, finishing with a partner change into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate Abanico on 1-2-3 by leading the follower's turn and stepping into the fan-like circular check on 5-6-7.
Complete the Abanico unwrapping turn on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), and instead of closing in Dile Que No, transition on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) into the Cadeneta chain with the next follower.
On counts 17-24, weave counter-clockwise through the Cadeneta on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, pick up the final follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Follow the opening Abanico turn on 1-2-3 and walk around the leader in the circular fan trajectory on 5-6-7.
Complete the Abanico turn on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and enter the Cadeneta weave on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) with the incoming leader.
On counts 17-24, continue weaving clockwise from leader to leader on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, connect with the final leader on 1-2-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: Maintain a thumb-free hook grip during the Abanico turns and Cadeneta transitions to prevent wrist twisting.
Forgetting to transition into the Cadeneta on count 13 and accidentally doing a standard Dile Que No after Abanico.
Letting the Abanico take too much space in the center before the chain begins.
variations: Shorter 3-eight-count version if Abanico is condensed into 1.5 eight-counts.
notes: UNSURE: Verify the exact eight-count length of your school's Abanico entry (2 vs 3 eight-counts before the Cadeneta).

name: Adentro y Afuera
summary: A dynamic group Rueda figure where all couples pulse or turn inward toward the center of the circle ('adentro') on the first eight-count and open back out toward the perimeter ('afuera') on the second eight-count before resuming or changing partners.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea or closed hold, lead the follower (or step together) inward toward the center of the Rueda on 1-3 ('adentro') and check/turn in the middle on 5-7.
Guide the partnership back outward toward the perimeter ('afuera') on 1-3 and resolve with a clean Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Follow the leader's frame inward toward the center of the circle on 1-3 ('adentro') and execute a compact check or turn in the middle on 5-7.
Step back outward toward the perimeter on 1-3 ('afuera') and walk smoothly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Taking oversized lunges into the center of a tight Rueda and colliding with neighbouring couples.
Confusing 'adentro' (inward) with 'afuera' (outward) on count 1.
Losing the circular alignment of the ring when returning to the perimeter.
variations: Adentro y Afuera con Dame (switching to the next follower on the outward return).
notes: UNSURE: Some schools teach 'Adentro y Afuera' as an Enchufla into the center followed by an outward turn, while others teach it as a closed-hold sweep in and out. Teacher should verify BOH Studios' version.

name: Adiós Doble
summary: An advanced Rueda partner-change figure that chains a double Adiós (Prima) pass—or an Adiós pass with two consecutive followers—before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Adiós (Prima) on 1-3, crossing and ducking under your raised left arm, then rebound on 5-7 into a second Adiós pass (or pass to the next follower 'la hermana').
Complete the second underarm Adiós pass on 1-3 and transition to the target follower on 5-7.
Collect the follower in semi-closed frame on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Step forward/in-place on 1-3 as the leader passes across for the first Adiós, and maintain frame for the rebound on 5-7.
Frame the second Adiós pass on 1-3 and hold your perimeter station on 5-7.
Connect with the incoming leader on 1-3 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Ducking by bending the neck forward instead of lowering with the knees on both passes.
Yanking the follower's left arm during the rebound between the first and second Adiós.
variations: Adiós Doble con la Familia.
notes: Ensure tall leaders use deep knee flexion rather than rounding the upper spine on both duck-unders.

name: Aguajea
summary: A swaggering, playful walking or basic variation where both dancers add Cuban street attitude ('aguaje'), shoulder rolls, and syncopated weight checks while circling each other.

leaderSteps.text: From open or one-hand connection, step 1-2-3 with a grounded knee bounce and thoracic shoulder roll, inviting the follower to mirror the groove.
Circle clockwise on 5-6-7 with stylized Cuban walks or a playful hesitation check before reconnecting in Guapea.

followerSteps.text: Match the leader's open groove on 1-2-3, adding hip figure-8 action and expressive free-arm or shoulder styling.
Circle opposite the leader on 5-6-7 with confident posture and reconnect on count 7.

commonMistakes: Looking at the floor instead of maintaining playful eye contact with your partner.
Losing the 1-2-3, 5-6-7 footwork pulse while focusing on upper-body styling.
Stiffening the knees.
variations: Inserting Aguajea mid-Setenta or after Vacílala when the music drops into a playful pregón.
notes: UNSURE: 'Aguajea' comes from 'aguaje' (Cuban swagger/showmanship). Check if BOH Studios teaches a specific choreographed footwork pattern for Aguajea or uses it as a styled Paseo/Guapea break.

name: Al Centro (Al Medio)
summary: From closed position (or open hold), all couples pulse their steps in and out toward the center of the Rueda circle ('al medio'), tightening and expanding the ring together with the music.

leaderSteps.text: Step left foot sideways/inward toward the exact center of the Rueda on 1-2, and tap/collect right foot on 3 (or rock 1-2-3 toward the center).
Step right foot outward back toward the perimeter of the circle on 5-6, and collect on 7.
Repeat the inward pulse on 9-11 and outward return on 13-15 until the caller calls the next figure.

followerSteps.text: In closed hold facing the leader, step right foot sideways/inward toward the center of the Rueda on 1-2-3, matching the group's contraction.
Step left foot outward back to the perimeter on 5-6-7.
Continue pulsing in (9-11) and out (13-15) with Cuban hip motion until the next call.

commonMistakes: Stepping out on count 1 when everyone else is stepping in toward the center.
Bumping hips in the middle when the Rueda circle is small; adjust step size to the circle diameter.
Losing the 1-2-3, 5-6-7 rhythm.
variations: Al Medio con Una / Dos / Tres (clapping or hip bumping on the center beat).
notes: Maps directly to the canonical 'Al Medio' enum value in the Rueda call list.

name: Alarde
summary: The 'Show-Off / Boast': an intermediate Rueda call where an Enchufla or Setenta wrap includes a dramatic free-arm styling flourish ('alarde'—running a hand behind the head/neck or chest pop) before switching partners into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a crisp Enchufla or Setenta entry on 1-2-3.

As you exchange places on 5-6-7, release one hand to execute the 'Alarde' show-off gesture (sweeping the free hand smoothly over your head/neck with Cuban swagger) while advancing toward the next follower.
Connect with the new follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn cleanly through the 1-2-3 entry.
Match the 'Alarde' styling on 5-6-7 with a confident hair/neck sweep and ribcage isolation on the perimeter.
Step back on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Focusing so much on the arm styling that your feet stop stepping on 5-6-7.
Arriving late to the next partner on count 9.
variations: Setenta con Alarde (performing the Alarde arm sweep while holding the follower in the Setenta hammerlock).
notes: Hand signal: caller sweeps an open hand behind the back of the head/neck.

name: Americano / Americana
summary: A playful Rueda call where the leader (Americano) or follower (Americana) executes a reverse-side or right-to-right/left-to-left underarm pass and check before resolving into Dile Que No (often with a partner change).

leaderSteps.text: From open hold, initiate an Enchufla-style or cross-hand lead on 1-2-3, turning yourself under the raised arm for 'Americano' (or turning the follower on the opposite side for 'Americana').
Complete the place exchange on 5-6-7, releasing or switching hands cleanly to face the next follower (or your current follower, per house call).
Collect the partner on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Step 1-2-3 in your circular frame as the leader turns under the arm for 'Americano' (or execute the reverse-side turn for 'Americana').
Maintain your spot on the outer perimeter on 5-6-7 with a clean basic check.
Step back on 9-11 and travel through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Forcing the shoulder backwards when turning under the 'wrong' (Americano) side; keep the elbow in front of the torso.
Mixing up who turns on 'Americano' (leader) versus 'Americana' (follower).
variations: Chaining Americano (1-8) directly into Americana (9-16).
notes: UNSURE: 'Americano/Americana' varies significantly across Rueda schools (sometimes a reverse Enchufla, sometimes a Cero/cross-body style pass). Teacher must verify BOH Studios' choreography.

name: Amistad
summary: The 'Friendship' call: an intermediate two-hand cross-hold Rueda figure where leaders and followers weave through an interconnected handshake wrap and exchange places to the next partner into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Take a right-to-right handshake hold (or crossed two-hand hold) and lead an Enchufla-style turn on 1-2-3.
Pass under or unwrap the 'friendship' handshake connection on 5-6-7 while stepping anticlockwise toward the next follower.
Collect the new follower on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn left on 1-2-3 while keeping a soft, rotating handshake hook.
Follow the secondary unwrap pass on 5-6-7 on the outer circle.
Connect with the incoming leader on 9-11 and travel through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Gripping the handshake with a locked thumb during the overhead turn; always use a loose finger hook.
Pulling the partner off balance during the release on count 7.
variations: Amistad Complicada (adding an extra leader turn before switching partners).
notes: UNSURE: 'Amistad' is taught as a right-to-right handshake wrap in some syllabi and a group neighbour embrace in others. Teacher should verify BOH Studios' version.

name: Amistad Complicada
summary: An intricate multi-couple Rueda weave building on the 'Amistad' handshake connection, combining cross-hand Enchuflas, follower exchanges with the neighbouring couple, and a partner change at the end.

leaderSteps.text: Switch to a right-to-right handshake hold on 1-2-3, lead an Enchufla with a leader turn or behind-the-back hand change on 5-6-7.
Lead the follower into a wrap or check on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), then release her to interact or swap with the neighbouring follower on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, receive the incoming follower in right-to-right hold on 1-2-3 and lead an inside turn with a dual-hand wrap on 5-6-7.
Unwind the follower on 1-2-3 (counts 25-27) and finish with a clean Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 29-31).

followerSteps.text: Connect right-to-right on 1-2-3 and turn left in the Enchufla on 5-6-7 while maintaining frame awareness.
Step into the check on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and travel to the neighbouring leader on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, connect with the new leader on 1-2-3 and turn smoothly into the wrap on 5-6-7, keeping elbows down in the safe zone.
Unwind on 1-2-3 (counts 25-27) and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 29-31).

commonMistakes: Safety: Forcing the follower's arm behind her back during the wrap or right-to-right turn—keep the hand at waist level and release immediately if timing is lost.
Starting with standard left-to-right hold instead of the 'Amistad' right-to-right handshake hold.
Losing the circle geometry during the partner exchange.
variations: Returning to the original partner on counts 17-24 before doing a final Dame.
notes: UNSURE: 'Amistad Complicada' is a school-specific combination whose exact sequence of wraps and neighbour swaps varies across instructors. Teacher must verify the exact 8-count choreography and whether it ends with a partner change.

name: Arrollao (Conga Comparsa Walk)
summary: The infectious Cuban carnival street-parade step ('arrollar' to the conga rhythm): three grounded marching steps followed by a syncopated hip/heel accent ('el golpe') on the '&-4' and '&-8'.

leaderSteps.text: Walk forward or in a circle with bent knees on left (1), right (2), left (3), then hit a sharp right-foot brush/kick or lateral hip accent on the '&-4' conga bombo beat.
Continue marching on right (5), left (6), right (7), and hit the left-foot brush/hip accent on the '&-8' conga beat while rolling the shoulders.

followerSteps.text: Step left (1), right (2), left (3) with carnival energy and grounded Cuban hip motion, hitting the syncopated hip/foot accent on '&-4'.
Step right (5), left (6), right (7) and hit the opposing hip/foot accent on '&-8' with joyful arm and shoulder styling.

commonMistakes: Missing the syncopated conga 'golpe' accent on the '&-4' / '&-8'.
Marching like a soldier with stiff legs instead of rolling the pelvis and shoulders.
variations: Forming a conga line ('arrollando') around the perimeter of the Rueda circle during a carnival/comparsa section.
notes: Whenever a Timba band drops into a carnival conga rhythm (like in Los Van Van or Havana D'Primera), Cuban dancers immediately switch to El Arrollao.

name: Babalú Ayé (Orisha of Healing, Earth & Lazarus)
summary: Sacred dance vocabulary of Babalú Ayé (syncretized with San Lázaro), the deeply revered Orisha of healing, infectious illness, humility, and miraculous recovery—danced with grounded, limping steps and the sweeping motion of the ja (palm-rib broom).

leaderSteps.text: Adopt a humble, bent posture on 1-3 and 5-7, stepping with a rhythmic, weighted limp while sweeping the 'ja' (sacred bundle of coconut/palm ribs) across your arms and legs to brush away illness.
As the rhythm intensifies, gradually rise from the afflicted posture into strong, vital torso contractions on 1-3 and 5-7, symbolizing miraculous healing and resilience.

followerSteps.text: Step with grounded, asymmetrical weight transfers on 1-3 and 5-7, using the hands to mime holding the 'ja' broom and cleansing the body and earth.
Channel deep emotional reverence through the torso contractions on 1-3 and 5-7 as the movement transitions toward strength and renewal.

commonMistakes: CRITICAL RESPECT NOTE: Never exaggerate Babalú Ayé's limping step as a joke or caricature—he is one of the most sacred and beloved figures in Cuba (celebrated every December 17 at El Rincón).
Losing the underlying 6/8 or Arará rhythmic pulse.
variations: Arará shoulder-shimmy variations (from the Dahomean/Arará tradition strongly associated with Babalú Ayé in Matanzas).
notes: Sacred in Regla de Ocha and Arará traditions: Babalú Ayé wears sackcloth/burlap (yute) with purple and royal/black-and-white beads; his attributes are the 'ja' (palm broom), crutches, and two dogs.

name: Babosa
summary: The 'Slug / Snail': a playful Rueda figure where the leader slides an arm or hand slowly and smoothly along the follower's arm/shoulder (or executes a slow body wave) during an Enchufla transition before switching partners.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, bringing the follower across.
As you pass on 5-6-7, glide your hand smoothly along the follower's shoulder/arm (the 'babosa' trail) while stepping toward the next follower.
Connect with the next follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Add a smooth body wave or shoulder isolation on 5-6-7 as the leader passes to the next station.
Step back on 9-11 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pressing heavily on the follower's neck or shoulder during the slide; keep the touch feather-light and respectful.
Lingering too long on count 7 and missing count 9.
variations: Babosa staying with the same partner.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios teaches 'La Babosa' as an arm/shoulder slide or a slow body-roll Enchufla.

name: Balsero
summary: A dynamic, continuous-flow Casino combination where the leader guides the follower through a wave-like series of alternating overhead sweeps and turns around the circle.

leaderSteps.text: From a two-hand hold, lead an initial right turn for the follower on 1-3 while stepping to the side, then on 5-7 sweep the joined left arm over your own head as you exchange places.
Without stopping the circular momentum, lead a continuous outside turn on 1-3 and finish with a crisp Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right on 1-3 keeping both hands connected with soft elbows, then travel around the leader on 5-7 as the arms sweep overhead.
Maintain your own axis through the turn on 1-3 and step cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Yanking the overhead arm sweep when the partner is too far away; step close to the center of the circle so arms stay bent.
Clamping the thumbs during the two-hand rotation.
Stopping the feet while moving the arms.
variations: Repeating the wave/overhead loop for an extra eight-count during long montuno sections.
notes: UNSURE: 'El Balsero' has several regional choreographies (some include a rowing/wave arm motion or a specific Sombrero entry). Teacher should confirm BOH Studios' version.

name: Bayamo por Matanzas
summary: An advanced geographical combination that chains the sweeping circular travel and wrap of Bayamo with a Matanzas-style behind-the-back hand change or Rumba-inflected check.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate the Bayamo entry on 1-3 with a dynamic turn and rotational sweep, stepping around the follower on 5-7.
Execute the Matanzas transition: pass the connection behind the back (or through a low hammerlock switch) on 1-3 and lead a syncopated directional reversal on 5-7.
Unwind the wrap with a crisp overhead turn on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Follow the sweeping Bayamo entry on 1-3 and maintain continuous circular momentum on 5-7.
Keep your free hand ready at waist level to pick up the behind-the-back/hammerlock switch on 1-3, pivoting cleanly through the reversal on 5-7.
Complete the exit turn on 1-3 and step through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Blindly grabbing for the hand behind the back; present the palm clearly at waist height and never yank.
Losing the 1-2-3, 5-6-7 footwork rhythm while focusing on the complex hand change.
Drifting too far apart during the behind-the-back pass.
variations: Adding a Rumba Guaguancó shoulder/torso accent on counts 13-15 (in tribute to Matanzas, the cradle of Rumba).
notes: UNSURE: Regional advanced figure; teacher should check the exact count of the Matanzas hand switch used by Enrique.

name: Bloqueo (Body Block Accent in Timba Despelote)
summary: A sharp, percussive full-body or ribcage 'lock/stop' ('bloqueo') used during Timba Despelote and mambo breaks to hit staccato horn, timbal, or bass bomb accents.

leaderSteps.text: Groove in a low-grounded Despelote stance on 1-2, then hit a sudden, razor-sharp thoracic ribcage and pelvic 'lock' (bloqueo) on count 3 (or on the exact musical break).
Release the freeze into a fluid circular body roll on 5-6 and hit a second crisp bloqueo accent on count 7.

followerSteps.text: Flow through a circular cintura/ribcage isolation on 1-2 and snap into a clean, motionless bloqueo freeze on count 3 to punctuate the horn or drum hit.
Melt back into fluid Despelote motion on 5-6 and lock the second accent on 7 with engaged core muscles.

commonMistakes: Hitting the freeze with a tense, grimacing face instead of keeping the neck and expression relaxed.
Only stopping the feet while the arms keep drifting; a true bloqueo stops the ribcage, hips, and hands simultaneously for a split second.
variations: Triple Bloqueo (hitting three consecutive staccato horn punches on 1, 2, 3 before rolling out on 5-7).
notes: Contrast is everything in Timba: the sharper the bloqueo freeze, the smoother the circular roll right after it looks.

name: Botao (Follower's Answer to the Vacunao)
summary: In Rumba Guaguancó, the 'botao' is the follower's sharp, decisive defensive turn-away, skirt whip, or hip/hand deflection that blocks and 'throws off' the leader's vacunao attempt.

leaderSteps.text: Circle the follower in Guaguancó basic on 1-2-3, using upper-body decoys and pañuelo passes to look for an opening.
Launch a sharp vacunao gesture (hand, foot, or pelvic accent) on count 5 or 6, and smile/recover on 7 as the follower successfully blocks it with her botao.

followerSteps.text: Dance an inviting, open Guaguancó basic on 1-2-3 while keeping peripheral awareness on the leader's hands and hips.
The instant the leader initiates the vacunao on 5/6, execute 'el botao': snap your skirt/hand across your pelvis while pivoting your hips sharply away to close the door and deflect the gesture.

commonMistakes: Keeping the pelvis covered the entire dance instead of opening playfully on 1-3 and snapping the botao shut at the exact split-second of the vacunao.
Turning your back completely and losing sight of the leader.
variations: Following the defensive botao with a playful counter-laugh or shoulder shimmy.
notes: Builds directly on 'rumba-guaguanco-basics' by naming and drilling the follower's specific defensive mechanics.

name: Cadena
summary: The 'Chain': a continuous weaving Rueda progression where leaders travel anticlockwise and followers travel clockwise around the perimeter, alternating right-hand and left-hand passes until the caller calls Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla with your right hand on 1-3, then keep your left hand connected (or reach forward with your left hand) on 5-7 to pass the next incoming follower on the inside/outside track.
Continue weaving anticlockwise around the circle, alternating right-hand Enchufla passes on 1-3 and left-hand passes on 5-7.
Maintain smooth circular pacing through the third eight-count without pulling on passing wrists.
When the caller shouts 'Dile Que No' (or 'Con esa'), collect the current follower on 1-3 and lead Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn through the initial right-hand Enchufla on 1-3, then offer your left hand to the next incoming leader on 5-7 as you travel clockwise around the circle.
Weave continuously clockwise around the perimeter, alternating right-hand turns on 1-3 and left-hand passes on 5-7.
Keep your steps compact and elbows soft through each hand-to-hand exchange.
On the exit call, step back on 1-3 with the leader in front of you and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Clamping thumbs or yanking passing arms as the chain speeds up; use a light palm/finger hook.
Offering the wrong hand (right instead of left on 5-7) and breaking the chain.
Collapsing the circle into an oval.
variations: Cadena Corta (stopping after passing 3 partners).
notes: One of the most joyful group-flow figures in Rueda de Casino; remind dancers to keep their eyes up to see the next hand coming.

name: Cadena Complicada
summary: An intertwined Rueda chain where leaders and followers weave around the circle alternating Enchufla turns and back-to-back or hand-change passes, resulting in a partner change down the line.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 with the current partner, then instead of settling into Dile Que No, step forward along the circle on 5-6-7 to catch the next follower's right hand (or left hand) and turn her past.
Execute a leader turn or behind-the-back hand change on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) as the next follower passes, then collect the following partner and finish with Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the opening Enchufla on 1-2-3, then travel clockwise along the circle on 5-6-7 while turning under the next leader's raised arm.
Continue weaving to the next leader on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) with a turn, then connect into closed hold on count 12 and complete Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Safety: Gripping the partner's thumb or twisting the wrist during the travelling turns—always use a hook grip without thumb pressure so hands can rotate freely.
Losing the circular geometry of the Rueda and collapsing into the center during the chain.
Forgetting to count how many partners are passed before the Dile Que No exit.
variations: Continuous Cadena until the caller shouts 'Dile Que No'.
notes: UNSURE: 'Cadena Complicada' varies widely between schools (some weave left- and right-hand Enchuflas continuously, others link Enchufla with an arm-hook switch). Teacher should confirm exact hand holds and total eight-counts.

name: Cadera (Cuban Hip Action from the Knees)
summary: The mechanics of authentic Cuban figure-8 hip motion ('cadera' / 'cintura'), generated naturally by alternating knee flexion and full floor-pressure weight transfers rather than forcing the hips separately.

leaderSteps.text: Step onto the ball of the left foot with a bent left knee on 1, press the heel down to straighten/settle the left hip on '&-2', and transfer weight through right (2) and left (3) in a compact figure-8.
Repeat on the right side on 5-6-7: bend the knee as the foot receives weight, then allow the hip to rotate back-and-around as the knee settles.

followerSteps.text: Step right (1), left (2), right (3) keeping knees soft and feet close together so each weight transfer naturally creates a figure-8 pendulum in the pelvis.
Step left (5), right (6), left (7), letting the hip settle fully on 3-4 and 7-8 while keeping the upper torso calm and decoupled.

commonMistakes: Pushing the hips out to the side artificially without transferring weight onto the foot first.
Dancing with straight, locked knees (which makes natural Cuban hip motion biomechanically impossible).
Tilting the shoulders from side to side with the hips.
variations: Cintura circular rolls (full 360-degree pelvic circles during Despelote).
notes: Rule #1 of Cuban motion: the hip movement is the result of the knee bend and floor pressure, never an isolated hula-hoop swing on locked legs.

name: Caja de Bolas
summary: The 'Ball Bearing': a classic Cuban Rueda formation call where dancers link hands in concentric or alternating rotating rings (leaders and followers rotating smoothly like a ball bearing) before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Step inward on 1-3 and link hands to form the 'Caja de Bolas' rotating ring structure on 5-7.
Rotate smoothly around the circle on 1-3 and 5-7 in coordination with the outer/inner ring.
Reverse or unwrap the ring structure cleanly on 1-3 and 5-7.
Collect the follower in front of you on 1-3 and lead Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Step into the perimeter/interlocking ring formation on 1-3 and 5-7 with soft elbows.
Travel smoothly along the circular track on 1-3 and 5-7, keeping even spacing between dancers.
Unwind from the ring structure on 1-3 and 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 with your new leader and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling on linked arms while the rings rotate; every dancer must propel their own weight with their feet.
Breaking the circle symmetry.
variations: Short 2-bar Caja de Bolas.
notes: UNSURE: 'Caja de bolas' (Cuban Spanish for ball bearing) is taught either as a concentric rotating ring formation or a continuous multi-turn knot. Verify with Enrique.

name: Cambio de Pareja
summary: 'Change Partner / Role Swap!': depending on caller convention, either an immediate partner switch around the circle OR a role-swap call where leader and follower trade leading/following positions within the couple.

leaderSteps.text: On 'Cambio de Pareja', step 1-2-3 to execute the switch (either advancing anticlockwise to the next partner or swapping sides/roles with your current partner per house rule).
Establish the new frame cleanly on 5-6-7 (or complete Dile Que No).

followerSteps.text: Execute the 1-2-3 transition on the perimeter (or step into the swapped role).
Connect in the new frame on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Hesitating on count 1 and getting caught between stations.
Pulling the partner's arm during the switch.
variations: Calling a second 'Cambio de Pareja' to switch roles back.
notes: UNSURE: In some European/Cuban Rueda schools 'Cambio de pareja' is a role-reversal (leader becomes follower, follower becomes leader), while in others it is a direct partner switch. Verify BOH Studios' house rule.

name: Camina
summary: A circular walking progression call in closed or semi-open Rueda hold where leaders walk forward clockwise (or guide the followers in a brisk circular walk) around the perimeter before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From closed position or after an Enchufla pickup, angle your frame along the line of the circle and walk briskly on left (1), right (2), left (3).
Continue the rhythmic circular walk on right (5), left (6), right (7), keeping the Rueda circle evenly spaced.
Check the walking momentum on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Match the leader's circular walking direction on 1-2-3 with smooth Cuban weight transfers and connected frame.
Continue walking along the perimeter on 5-6-7 without letting the distance to the couple ahead widen.
Feel the leader's check on 9-11 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Overtaking the couple in front of you and stepping on their heels.
Walking with stiff knees instead of a grounded Cuban stride.
variations: Camina y Dame (releasing the walk directly into a partner change).
notes: UNSURE: Some schools use 'Camina' synonymously with 'Me La Llevo' (fast closed-hold walking around the circle), while others use it as a 3-step forward walk inside a turn pattern. Verify with Enrique.

name: Caminando (Walking Basic with Arms)
summary: A solo traveling or in-place walking shine that coordinates grounded Cuban footwork with natural, opposing ribcage and arm swing.

leaderSteps.text: Step forward on left (1), right (2), left (3) with knees flexed, allowing the right shoulder and bent right forearm to swing naturally forward in opposition to the left leg.
Step backward or curve around on right (5), left (6), right (7), alternating the natural Cuban arm and torso opposition on each step.

followerSteps.text: Walk forward or in a compact circle on right (1), left (2), right (3), rolling through the ball of each foot and coordinating graceful opposing arm motion.
Continue walking or step back on left (5), right (6), left (7), letting the hips settle over each weighted step.

commonMistakes: Swinging the same arm and leg forward at the same time ('robot walking') instead of using natural contralateral opposition.
Locking the knees on weight transfer.
Holding the hands dead and stiff at the sides.
variations: Caminando en Círculo (walking a full 360-degree solo circle over 1-3 and 5-7).
notes: Essential warmup drill for teaching students how the upper body and arms move organically from the ground up.

name: Candado
summary: The 'Padlock': a signature intermediate knot figure where a two-hand wrap locks both arms around the follower (or shared frame) before unlocking through sequential overhead turns into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From a two-hand hold, lead the follower into a right hammerlock turn on 1-3 as in Setenta.
Instead of releasing or unwrapping, drape the second arm over the follower's head/shoulder on 5-6-7 so the follower is framed in the 'padlock' (Candado) wrap while you step around the circle.
Unlock the padlock by raising the top arm on 9-11 for the follower's unwind turn, and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn right on 1-3 into the hammerlock, keeping your right hand relaxed against your lower back.
Step compactly in place/around the circle on 5-6-7 as the second arm drapes over to form the Candado lock, keeping both shoulders relaxed.
Unwind smoothly on 9-11 as the leader lifts the arms in sequence, and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling on the locked hands while the follower is wrapped in Candado, which can torque both shoulders.
SAFETY: Lifting the arms in the wrong order on counts 9-11; always lift the top arm of the cross first.
Standing too far from the follower during the wrap.
variations: Candado Complicado (adding a leader duck-under while the follower stays in the lock).
notes: Crucial safety cue for leaders: keep a tiny circular radius during Candado so the follower's elbows stay comfortably bent.

name: Cangrejo
summary: The 'Crab': an intermediate Rueda call where couples bend their knees into a low stance and walk sideways/diagonally with syncopated crab-like steps ('cangrejo') and pincer hand gestures before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From open hold or Enchufla, lower your center of gravity and step sideways along the circle on 1-2-3 like a crab.
Continue the lateral crab walk on 5-6-7 (adding playful crab-claw hand snaps if called) toward the next follower.
Rise back to normal Casino posture on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Lower into a soft knee bend and step sideways on 1-2-3 matching the crab rhythm.
Complete the second lateral crab phrase on 5-6-7 on the outer circle.
Connect with the leader on 9-11 and travel through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Bending at the lower back instead of keeping the torso upright and bending at the knees and hips.
Stepping onto neighboring dancers' feet during the sideways travel.
variations: Cangrejo in closed hold around the circle.
notes: Great lower-body quad and hip conditioning inside a playful Rueda call.

name: Carousel con Sabor
summary: A dynamic Rueda wheel figure where dancers link into a rotating central carousel (star/wheel formation), revolve around the circle with stylized Cuban 'sabor' body movement accents, and release to a new partner in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 to bring the couple toward the center, and on 5-6-7 link hands/wrists in the middle to form the rotating Carousel wheel with the follower positioned on the outer spoke.
Walk forward in the rotating wheel on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and pause/groove on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) with a synchronized 'con sabor' hip/ribcage isolation or vocal accent.
On counts 17-24, continue or reverse the Carousel rotation on 1-2-3 and lead the follower through an underarm turn on 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, release the center wheel, pick up the next follower on 1-2-3, and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the Enchufla on 1-2-3 and connect into the outer spoke of the Carousel wheel on 5-6-7.
Walk along the outer circumference on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) matching the inner wheel's angular speed, and hit the 'con sabor' body movement break on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, walk with the wheel on 1-2-3 and turn cleanly under the connected arm on 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, connect with the incoming leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: In a multi-person Carousel wheel, never lock fingers or pull downward on linked wrists—if the wheel moves too fast for the outer ring, release immediately.
Leaders in the inner ring taking massive steps, forcing followers on the outer ring to sprint.
Missing the synchronized 'sabor' break on counts 13-15.
variations: Followers forming the inner wheel while leaders travel on the outside.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether 'Carousel con Sabor' in your curriculum forms a central star wheel or an individual couple rodeo/carousel spin.

name: Cero
summary: The 'Zero': after an Enchufla entry, the leader traces a complete 360-degree circular loop ('0') around the follower (or around the next partner) before picking up in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Enchufla on 1-2-3, trading places with your follower.
Release hands and briskly walk a full circular loop ('zero') around the follower on 5-6-7 (or through 9-11), passing behind her back and around her front.
Complete the circular orbit on 9-11 to arrive in front of the follower (or next follower) and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Stay anchored on your spot on the perimeter on 5-6-7, dancing a compact basic or hip groove while the leader circles around you.
Connect with the leader as he completes the loop on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Followers stepping backward or traveling while the leader is circling closely behind their back, causing tripped heels.
Leaders taking too wide a circle and arriving late on count 11.
variations: Ocho (tracing a figure-8 loop around both your current follower and the next follower).
notes: Hand signal: caller draws a circle ('0') in the air with an index finger or forms an 'O' with thumb and index finger. Confirm whether BOH Studios keeps the same partner or switches on Cero.

name: Cero Doble
summary: A Rueda call where the leader initiates an Enchufla, circles completely around the follower twice (two full 'zero' loops) while she marks time in place, and finishes with a partner change via Dame on the final eight-count.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 to swap places, then instead of going to the next partner, circle all the way around your current follower's back on 5-6-7 to complete the first loop ('un cero').
Continue jogging/stepping smoothly in a second full circle around the same follower on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) to complete the double zero.
On counts 17-24, travel onward to the next follower on the right on 1-2-3 and lead her through a Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the opening Enchufla on 1-2-3, then mark basic steps in place on 5-6-7 (often tapping the index finger to the temple or tracing a '0' in the air) while the leader circles around you.
Continue marking Cuban basic in place with hip movement on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) as the leader completes his second orbit.
On counts 17-24, step in place on 1-2-3 to receive the incoming leader from the left and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Followers travelling or turning out of place while the leader is trying to circle around them, making the orbit too wide.
Leaders running out of rhythm and colliding with neighbouring leaders in tight Ruedas.
Forgetting whether Cero ends with the same partner or advances to the next partner on the final count.
variations: Cero con alarde (followers styling with afro/rumba shoulders while leaders circle).
notes: UNSURE: Some schools execute both orbits faster within 2 eight-counts (one loop on 5-7, second loop on 9-11, Dile Que No on 13-15), and some keep the same partner unless 'con dame' is called. Confirm whether your school uses 2 or 3 eight-counts and whether it changes partner.

name: Chachachá Cubano Basics
summary: Created by Cuban violinist Enrique Jorrín in the early 1950s: danced on contratiempo (breaking on 2 and 6) with a compact, grounded triple-step shuffle ('cha-cha-chá' on 4-and-1 / 8-and-5) and playful knees-bent groove.

leaderSteps.text: Step left foot in place on 1 (finishing the triple step), rock right foot back/forward on 2, replace weight onto left foot on 3, and shuffle right-left-right ('cha-cha-chá') compactly under your hips on 4-and-5.
Complete the shuffle onto right foot on 5, rock left foot forward/back on 6, replace weight onto right foot on 7, and shuffle left-right-left ('cha-cha-chá') on 8-and-1.

followerSteps.text: Mirror the leader: finish the shuffle on right foot on 1, rock left foot forward/back on 2, replace weight onto right foot on 3, and dance a compact left-right-left chassé on 4-and-5.
Land on left foot on 5, rock right foot back/forward on 6, replace weight onto left on 7, and shuffle right-left-right on 8-and-1 with soft knees.

commonMistakes: Snapping the legs straight like international ballroom Cha-Cha instead of keeping the knees soft and brushing the floor ('dragging the feet') in authentic Cuban style.
Breaking on count 1 instead of count 2.
variations: Crossing the feet or hopping lightly during the 'cha-cha-chá' triple step in solo shines.
notes: Enrique Jorrín named the dance after the whispering sound of dancers' shoes brushing the floor on the triple step ('cha-cha-chá').

name: Changüí Basics
summary: Originating in Guantánamo (eastern Cuba) as the direct ancestor of Son Cubano: a grounded, syncopated dance characterized by a lower knee bend, accented off-beat steps, and driving marímbula/bongó de monte energy.

leaderSteps.text: Sink slightly lower into the knees than in Havana Son, stepping with a syncopated lateral/rotational bounce and sharp heel-ball weight checks on 1-3 and 5-7.
In closed or one-hand hold, guide the follower in tight clockwise circular steps on 1-3 and 5-7 while accenting the syncopated upbeats with your shoulders and torso.

followerSteps.text: Match the grounded, syncopated Changüí pulse on 1-3 and 5-7 with pronounced knee flexion and rhythmic hip accents.
Rotate closely with the leader on 1-3 and 5-7, keeping your steps compact and earthy.

commonMistakes: Dancing Changüí tall and stiff like ballroom Danzón instead of feeling its earthy, syncopated Guantánamo groove.
Taking long linear steps.
variations: Breaking into solo Changüí syncopated footwork shines when Elito Revé y su Charangón plays.
notes: Essential whenever dancing to Elito Revé y su Charangón ('El Changüí de Guantánamo')!

name: Coca-Cola con Puente y Arriba
summary: A Rueda figure combining a Dile Que No with Coca-Cola turn, a two-hand overhead bridge ('puente') that the leader ducks under, and a reverse progression upstream ('arriba', clockwise) to change partners.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a Dile Que No on 1-2-3 and guide the follower into the sweeping 360-degree Coca-Cola turn on 5-6-7.

Connect both hands overhead to form an arch ('puente') on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), duck cleanly underneath the bridge while turning on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15), and release toward the upstream ('arriba', clockwise) follower.
On counts 17-24, connect with the previous/upstream follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through a Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Step through the opening preparation on 1-2-3 and execute the sweeping counter-clockwise Coca-Cola turn across the slot on 5-6-7.
Maintain rounded, supportive arms overhead to form the 'puente' on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) while the leader ducks underneath on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, receive the leader arriving from the upstream ('arriba') direction on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: Leaders must bend at the knees and keep the spine vertical when ducking under the 'puente' arch, never pulling down on the follower's raised arms.
Moving in the standard Dame direction (counter-clockwise) instead of 'arriba' (clockwise/upstream).
Cutting the Coca-Cola turn short on 5-6-7.
variations: Keeping the same partner and walking together 'arriba' if no partner change is intended.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether 'con puente y arriba' in your school means the leader ducks under a bridge and advances 'arriba' (to the previous partner), or whether 'arriba' refers to continuous walking up the circle. Includes duck-under safety guidance.

name: Compota
summary: An advanced, multi-layered Rueda knot figure ('stew / fruit compote') combining a Setenta hammerlock, an overhead Sombrero/Siete switch, and a partner change into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Enter with a two-hand Setenta hammerlock on 1-3 and lead a cross-body/circular exchange on 5-7 while retaining both hands.
Execute the 'Compota' arm-knot switch on 1-3 and unwind the follower overhead on 5-7 while stepping toward the next follower.
Collect the next follower on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right into the hammerlock on 1-3 and travel across on 5-7 with a soft right elbow.
Follow the continuous two-hand knot unwrap on 1-3 and 5-7 with a loose two-finger hook grip.
Step back on 1-3 with the incoming leader and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Clamping thumbs during the multi-turn wrist switches.
Stepping too far away while both hands are wrapped.
variations: Compota staying with the same partner.
notes: UNSURE: Verify exact count-by-count hand switches for Compota with Enrique.

name: Consorte
summary: An intermediate Rueda figure where the leader wraps the follower into a side-by-side promenade ('consorte' / companion hold), walks or turns together, and transitions to the next partner into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From open hold, lead the follower into a side-by-side sweetheart/companion wrap on 1-2-3.
Promenade or pivot together on 5-6-7, then release the follower outward as you advance anticlockwise.
Pick up the next follower on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn into the side-by-side companion wrap on 1-2-3 with soft elbows.
Walk/pivot with the leader on 5-6-7, unwinding cleanly onto the outer perimeter on count 7.
Connect with the incoming leader on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling the follower's wrapped arms behind her shoulder line.
Releasing the wrap too late on count 8.
variations: Consorte staying with the same partner.
notes: UNSURE: Regional definitions of 'Consorte' vary; teacher should confirm BOH Studios' exact handhold and whether it changes partner.

name: Contra Mambo
summary: A musical Rueda call where couples rock in opposition (or on syncopated contratiempo counts) during a Mambo break, creating a push-and-pull visual contrast around the circle before resolving.

leaderSteps.text: In closed or two-hand frame, step back/side on 1-2-3 while guiding the follower in counter-motion (or stepping on the syncopated contratiempo upbeat).
Reverse the counter-mambo rock on 5-6-7 with strong ribcage isolation.
Re-establish standard A Tiempo frame on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Match the leader's counter-directional (or contratiempo) Mambo step on 1-2-3 with active core tension.
Execute the opposing Mambo rock on 5-6-7.
Step back on 9-11 and travel smoothly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Letting the arms go limp so the counter-directional rock feels mushy.
Failing to lock back onto count 1 when exiting the Contra Mambo.
variations: Contra Mambo con Dame (switching partners on the exit).
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios teaches 'Contra Mambo' as opposing footwork directions (one forward, one back) or as a contratiempo (On2) rhythm shift.

name: Cruce
summary: The 'Cross-Over': after an Enchufla on 1-3, every leader walks straight across the center diameter of the Rueda circle on 5-7 to pick up the follower directly opposite them for Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Enchufla on 1-2-3 and release connection.
Spot the follower directly opposite you across the center of the Rueda and walk briskly across the middle on 5-6-7, passing other leaders by the right shoulder.
Collect the opposite follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Complete the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Stay anchored on your perimeter station on 5-6-7, looking straight across the center of the circle to spot your incoming leader.
Connect with the arriving leader on 9-11 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Leaders running through the exact center point without yielding right-of-way (pass right-shoulder-to-right-shoulder in the middle to avoid collisions!).
Two leaders claiming the same follower in an odd-numbered Rueda circle.
variations: Cruce con Alarde.
notes: Works best when the Rueda has an even number of couples (4, 6, or 8 couples) so every leader has an exact opposite station.

name: Cubanita
summary: The counterpart to Cubanito where the follower is guided through the window/duck-under wrap while the leader frames the rotation around the circle.

leaderSteps.text: Start as in Cubanito or Enchufla on 1-3, raising the joined arm to create a clear, high window for the follower.
Guide the follower through the window/turn on 5-6-7 while stepping compactly around the outside of the circle.
Release the overhead wrap smoothly on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Step 1-2-3 into the Enchufla exchange, keeping your frame connected and eyes up.
Pass cleanly under the raised arm window on 5-6-7 by bending your knees slightly and keeping your elbow in front of your ribcage.
Open out on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Forcing the follower's head or neck down under a low arm window; the leader must raise the window above head height.
Rushing the follower's exit before count 7.
Letting the elbow flare behind the shoulder line.
variations: Chaining Cubanito directly into Cubanita over 3-4 eight-counts.
notes: UNSURE: Regional variations exist between Havana and European Rueda syllabi on whether Cubanita uses a neck drape or a double-hand window. Verify with Enrique.

name: Cubanito
summary: A playful figure starting with a two-hand cross-hold or Enchufla entry where the leader ducks under the joined arms and wraps into a compact window before exiting with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From a right-to-right or crossed two-hand hold (right over left), lead an Enchufla-style exchange on 1-2 and duck under the raised right arm on 3, turning to face the follower.
Keep the right arm draped lightly over your own right shoulder/neck or turn the follower on 5-6-7 to trade places around the circle.
Unwind the arm wrap on 9-11 and lead a clean Dile Que No on 13-15 to return to open Guapea.

followerSteps.text: Step forward and pivot left on 1-3 as in Enchufla, keeping your right arm soft as the leader ducks underneath.
Walk around the leader in a tight circular arc on 5-6-7 (or execute the led inside turn) while maintaining a bent, tension-free elbow.
Step back on 9-11 to set the frame and travel through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling down on the partner's arm while ducking under, which strains the shoulder joint.
SAFETY: Ducking by bending at the waist with the head down instead of lowering with the knees and keeping the spine upright.
Standing too far apart during the arm wrap.
variations: Cubanito con Cubanita (alternating leader and follower duck-unders).
notes: UNSURE: Some schools teach Cubanito from a single right-to-right shake-hands hold (like El Dedo), while others use a two-hand hold. Teachers should confirm BOH Studios' preferred handhold.

name: Dame (Dame Una / Dame Otra)
summary: The foundational Rueda de Casino partner-change call where every leader releases their current follower on counts 1-3, travels anticlockwise along the inside of the circle, and picks up the next follower on 5-7 into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea, step left foot forward/open on 1, release your current follower completely on 2, and pivot left on 3 to face the next follower to your right (anticlockwise around the circle).
Collect the new follower in semi-closed hold on 5 and lead a clean Dile Que No on 5-6-7 to establish the new partnership facing the circle.

followerSteps.text: Step right foot back into your Guapea check on 1-2-3 while keeping your place on the perimeter of the Rueda circle and opening your frame toward the center.
Connect with the incoming leader arriving from your left on 5 and travel smoothly through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Followers walking forward along the circle to chase the new leader instead of holding their spot on 1-3.
Leaders cutting straight across the middle of a large Rueda instead of curving cleanly to the next partner.
Grabbing the new follower's arm on count 3 before arriving in front of her frame on count 5.
variations: Dame Otra (repeating Dame immediately on the next eight-count).
Dame con Una (adding one single clap on count 7 or 8).
notes: Hand signal: caller raises one index finger in the air (or points toward the next follower).

name: Dame Directo
summary: A fast, direct partner change in Rueda where leaders travel immediately to the next follower on their right on counts 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7 without a full Guapea rock step.

leaderSteps.text: Instead of stepping into a standard Guapea away from the partner, release the current follower and walk directly counter-clockwise around the inside of the circle toward the next follower on the right, establishing closed or Dile Que No hold by count 3. Pause on 4.
Lead the new follower through the second half of Dile Que No on 5-6-7, rotating counter-clockwise to face her in the new slot. Pause on 8.

followerSteps.text: Step in place or slightly forward along the circle edge on 1-2-3 while angling the torso toward the center to receive the incoming leader coming from the left. Pause on 4.
Travel across the new leader's slot in a standard Dile Que No trajectory on 5-6-7, pivoting on 7 to face the new partner. Pause on 8.

commonMistakes: Leaders taking too long to release the previous partner on count 1, arriving late to the new follower on count 5.
Followers walking backward out of the circle on 1-3 instead of holding the circumference of the Rueda.
Pulling the new follower's arm on count 3 before establishing a proper visual and frame connection.
variations: Chained consecutive Dame Directo calls ('Dame directo, directo, directo') where leaders change partners every single eight-count.
notes: UNSURE: Some schools call 'Dame Directo' when transitioning straight from a closed-hold figure into a partner change on 5-6-7 without an intervening Guapea, while others use it for rapid-fire 1-eight-count Dames. Confirm your school's exact trigger beat.

name: Dame Dos
summary: A Rueda partner-change call where the leader skips one follower and travels past her along the inside of the circle to pick up the second follower into Dile Que No on counts 5-7.

leaderSteps.text: Open from Guapea on 1, release your current partner, and take three brisk, grounded steps on 1-2-3 past the first follower on your right toward the second follower.
Arrive cleanly in front of the second follower before count 5, connect in semi-closed frame, and lead Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Execute your compact Guapea back-rock on 1-2-3 while staying anchored on the outer perimeter of the circle so passing leaders have a clear inside lane.
Connect with the new leader arriving on count 5 and travel smoothly through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Leaders sprinting blindly across the center and colliding; always travel along the inside arc of the circle with eyes up.
Arriving late on count 6 and yanking the new follower through a rushed Dile Que No.
Followers drifting inward into the leaders' travel lane on 1-3.
variations: Dame Dos con Dos (adding two claps on the transition).
notes: Hand signal: caller raises two fingers in a V-shape above the head.

name: Dame Dos con Cuba
summary: An advanced Rueda partner-change call where the leader skips one follower (Dame Dos) while inserting a syncopated Cuban Rumba/Guaguancó break or Enchufla check ('con Cuba') before picking up the second follower in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate the transition on 1-2-3, releasing your current follower and traveling past the first follower on your right.
Hit the 'con Cuba' Rumba Guaguancó isolation / syncopated check on 5-6-7 as you arrive at the second follower.
Connect with the second follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Hold your perimeter station on 1-2-3 as leaders travel two spots anticlockwise.
Execute the matching 'con Cuba' Rumba hip and shoulder isolation on 5-6-7.
Connect with the arriving leader on 9-11 and travel through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the first follower instead of skipping one for Dame Dos.
Rushing the Rumba isolation on 5-7.
variations: Dame Una con Cuba.
notes: Confirm whether BOH Studios uses 'con Cuba' as a 4-count Rumba break or a specific clap-and-hip check.

name: Dame Pa' Atrás
summary: A reverse Rueda partner-change call where, instead of moving anticlockwise to the next follower on the right, the leader steps backward/clockwise ('pa' atrás') to pick up the previous follower on their left into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea, release your current partner on 1 and step/pivot clockwise ('backwards' along the Rueda progression) on 1-2-3 toward the follower on your left.
Connect with that follower in semi-closed frame on 5 and lead Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Execute your Guapea back-check on 1-2-3 on the outer perimeter, looking to your right to spot the leader arriving from the reverse direction.
Receive the incoming leader on 5 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Leaders walking backward blindly without pivoting their head/shoulders to see the follower on their left.
Moving anticlockwise out of muscle memory and crashing into the neighbouring leader.
variations: Dame Dos Pa' Atrás (skipping one follower in the reverse clockwise direction).
notes: Hand signal: caller jerks a thumb backward over the shoulder.

name: Dame por la Mano
summary: A smooth, continuous partner-change variation of Dame where the leader retains or picks up hand-to-hand connection to turn/guide the follower cleanly during the transition into the next partnership.

leaderSteps.text: From Guapea or Enchufla, use a low or overhead left-to-right hand lead on 1-2-3 to guide/turn your current follower outward while you step anticlockwise toward the next follower.
Pick up the next follower by the hand/frame on 5 and lead Dile Que No (or a direct hand-turn pickup) on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Follow the leader's hand lead on 1-2-3 along the outer perimeter while keeping your free hand ready at waist level.
Connect with the incoming leader on 5 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Holding onto the first follower's hand past count 3 and pulling her arm as you walk to the next partner.
Grabbing the new partner's thumb instead of using a light hook connection.
variations: Dame con la Mano turning the incoming follower on 5-6-7 instead of Dile Que No.
notes: UNSURE: In some schools 'Dame por la Mano' means switching partners without Dile Que No (picking up directly in open Guapea hand-to-hand on 5-7). Teacher should confirm BOH Studios' definition.

name: Dame Rápido
summary: A fast-reflex Rueda partner-change call where leaders switch to the next follower immediately on counts 1-3 and resume Guapea (or execute an immediate turn) on 5-7 without a full two-bar transition.

leaderSteps.text: Release your current partner on 1 and travel briskly anticlockwise on 1-2-3 to arrive directly in front of the next follower by count 3.
Immediately lead Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (or connect directly into open Guapea on 5-6-7 if called during fast switches).

followerSteps.text: Keep your Guapea step ultra-compact on the outer rim on 1-2-3, spotting your left immediately.
Connect instantly with the arriving leader on 5 and execute Dile Que No (or open check) on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Hesitating on count 1 and arriving too late on count 5.
SAFETY: Yanking the new follower through Dile Que No to make up for late footwork.
variations: Calling three consecutive Dame Rápido switches in a row during a high-energy Timba mambo.
notes: Tests the Rueda's ability to keep a tight circle diameter so 3 steps are enough to reach the next partner.

name: Dame Rápido con Vuelta
summary: A high-speed Rueda partner change where leaders release their current partner immediately on count 1, execute a solo 360-degree travelling spin ('con vuelta') toward the next follower on 1-3, and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-7.

leaderSteps.text: Release the current partner immediately on count 1 and execute a travelling 360-degree turn counter-clockwise along the inside of the circle on 1-2-3 to arrive in front of the next follower by count 3. Pause on 4.
Connect smoothly with the new follower on count 4 and lead her across the slot in a Dile Que No on 5-6-7. Pause on 8.

followerSteps.text: Execute a solo turn in place along the perimeter on 1-2-3 (or hold a poised Guapea check facing the center) while spotting the incoming spinning leader. Pause on 4.
Connect in frame on count 4 and travel through a clean Dile Que No on 5-6-7 with the new leader. Pause on 8.

commonMistakes: Leaders spinning blindly on 1-2-3 without spotting the new follower, resulting in a rough or late grab on count 5.
Taking 2 eight-counts instead of executing the immediate 'rápido' change on counts 1-3.
Letting centrifugal force swing the elbows out during the travelling spin.
variations: Both leaders and followers turning on 1-3, or adding an Exhíbela turn for the follower on 5-6-7.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether 'con vuelta' applies to the leader spinning while travelling on 1-3, the follower turning during the Dile Que No on 5-7, or both.

name: Dame Una Arriba
summary: A reverse-direction Rueda partner-change call where the leader travels clockwise ('arriba' / upstream) to pick up the follower on their left into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea, step on 1 and immediately pivot right (clockwise) on 2-3, traveling upstream around the circle toward the follower on your left.
Connect with the new follower in semi-closed frame on 5 and lead Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Step 1-2-3 in place on the outer rim of the circle, turning your visual focus slightly to your right to spot the leader arriving from the 'arriba' direction.
Receive the leader's frame on 5 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Moving anticlockwise out of habit as in a standard Dame, causing a head-on collision with the neighboring leader.
Over-rotating on count 3 and arriving off-balance on count 5.
variations: Calling Dame Una Arriba from closed marching position (Vamos Arriba).
notes: UNSURE: Some schools only call 'Dame Arriba' while marching in closed position (Vamos Arriba), while others also call it from open Guapea. Teacher should verify BOH Studios' convention.

name: Dame Una con Una, Una con Dos
spanishName: Dame Una con Una, Una con Dos
summary: A two-part Rueda partner-change sequence combining a single Dame accented by one clap ('con una') followed immediately by a second Dame accented by a double clap ('con dos'), advancing the leader two partners in total.

leaderSteps.text: Step Guapea on 1-2-3, release the current follower, clap once sharply on count 4 (or count 7/8 per local convention), and travel counter-clockwise to lead the next follower through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.
Dance one basic Guapea and Dile Que No (or immediate transition) with the new partner to establish rhythm before the second half of the call.
On counts 17-24, initiate another Dame on 1-2-3, execute two quick claps ('con dos') during the transition, and collect the next follower down the line on 5-6-7.
Complete the Dile Que No with the final partner on counts 25-32 and settle into Guapea.

followerSteps.text: Step Guapea on 1-2-3, clap once with the group on the accented beat, and receive the new leader arriving from the left into Dile Que No on 5-6-7.
Complete the transition or stabilizing basic with the new partner.
On counts 17-24, step Guapea on 1-2-3, perform two crisp claps ('con dos'), and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 with the second incoming leader.
Finish the Dile Que No and re-establish Guapea frame on counts 25-32.

commonMistakes: Clapping out of time with the rest of the circle or letting the clap delay the footwork on count 5.
Confusing 'Dame una con dos' (advance 1 partner, clap 2 times) with 'Dame dos con una' (skip 1 partner to advance 2 partners, clap 1 time).
Leaders grabbing the new follower's arm late because their hands are still occupied clapping on count 5.
variations: Continuous seamless version in 2 eight-counts total (1-8 for 'Dame una con una', 9-16 directly into 'Una con dos').
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether your teachers execute the two Dames back-to-back in 2 eight-counts (1-8 and 9-16) or with a stabilizing basic in between (4 eight-counts), and whether the claps fall on count 4, count 7, or counts 7-8-1.

name: Danzón Basics
summary: Cuba's official national dance (born in Matanzas in 1879): an aristocratic, understated closed-position box/cajón step danced to the baqueteo rhythm, alternating with elegant 'paseo' resting/fanning promenades.

leaderSteps.text: In a poised, upright closed frame, trace a tiny, smooth box step ('el cajón'): step left foot side on 1, close right on 2, step left forward/back on 3 (pause 4); step right side on 5, close left on 6, step right back/forward on 7 (pause 8).
During the instrumental flute/violin 'paseo' bridge, pause the dance steps and walk/converse gallantly with your partner around the salon until the melody signals the return to closed hold.

followerSteps.text: Mirror the leader's compact Danzón box step on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7 with minimal hip exaggeration and regal Havana salon posture.
Stroll arm-in-arm with the leader during the 'paseo' rest section (traditionally fanning gently on the beat) before re-entering the closed embrace.

commonMistakes: Exaggerating wild Timba hip rolls during a refined Danzón.
Continuing to dance turn patterns through the traditional Danzón rest/paseo section.
variations: Transitioning from Danzón into Cha-Cha-Chá (which evolved directly from the final 'nuevo ritmo' mambo section of the Danzón).
notes: Historical connection for students: Danzón -> Danzonete -> Danzón-Mambo -> Cha-Cha-Chá -> Son/Casino.

name: Derecha / Izquierda
summary: 'Right / Left!': a rapid directional Rueda call where the entire circle travels or shifts partners laterally to the right ('Derecha') or to the left ('Izquierda') on command.

leaderSteps.text: On 'Derecha', step or slide laterally to your right (anticlockwise) on 1-2-3; on 'Izquierda', step or slide laterally to your left (clockwise) on 1-2-3.
Check weight and re-establish connection (or complete the partner pickup) on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Respond to the caller's directional command on 1-2-3, maintaining your spot on the perimeter or shifting in sync with the group rule.
Settle into frame on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Hesitating between left and right and stepping into the neighboring dancer.
Crossing the feet awkwardly instead of using clean lateral chassé steps.
variations: Alternating quick '¡Derecha! ¡Izquierda!' calls while in Al Medio.
notes: UNSURE: Verify whether BOH Studios uses 'Derecha / Izquierda' while facing the center in a single circle or as a partner-change direction.

name: ¡Dícelo!
summary: A high-energy Rueda call shouted right after a Dile Que No (or during a partner change), prompting the couple to repeat or accent the Dile Que No cross-slot walk with a vocal shout or playful attitude, without changing partners.

leaderSteps.text: From the end of the previous Dile Que No, step back-side-together on 1-2-3 while opening the frame and checking the follower into a second immediate Dile Que No preparation (or playful Guapea check). Pause on 4.
Lead the follower across the slot in a snappy Dile Que No on 5-6-7 while joining the circle's vocal call or clap accent. Pause on 8.

followerSteps.text: Instead of settling into a passive Guapea, use the momentum of the previous figure to rock back-side-together on 1-2-3 with engaged frame tension. Pause on 4.
Travel briskly across the slot in a Dile Que No arc on 5-6-7, adding Cuban hip motion and matching the vocal accent of the call. Pause on 8.

commonMistakes: Dropping the right-hand frame connection on count 8 of the previous Dile Que No, leaving no tension to initiate '¡Dícelo!' on count 1.
Pulling the follower's left hand on count 3 instead of leading from the right hand on her upper back.
Confusing '¡Dícelo!' with a partner change and releasing the follower.
variations: Adding a synchronized foot stomp or vocal shout ('¡Que no!') on count 1 or count 4.
notes: UNSURE: In some schools, '¡Dícelo!' is a call-and-response vocal/clap flourish or an immediate second Dile Que No ('Dile que no > ¡Dícelo!'), whereas in others it triggers a quick Vacílala or Sacala check. Verify the exact footwork response taught in Bournemouth.

name: Dile Que Sí
summary: The opposite of Dile Que No: the leader guides the follower from open Guapea position back into closed embrace along a smooth clockwise arc.

leaderSteps.text: Step left foot forward-and-slightly-side on 1, rock weight back to right on 2, and bring left foot underneath your hip on 3 while opening your right arm to invite the follower toward your right side.
Step right foot back/in-place on 5, rotate slightly clockwise on 6, and close left foot near right on 7 while placing your right hand gently onto the follower's left shoulder blade in closed hold.

followerSteps.text: Step right foot back-and-slightly-open on 1, transfer weight to left foot on 2, and step right foot forward toward the leader on 3.
Walk curved forward-and-around on left (5), right (6), and settle onto left foot on 7 directly in front of the leader, resting your left hand on the leader's right shoulder.

commonMistakes: Yanking the follower's right hand on count 1 instead of inviting them with torso rotation.
Walking in a straight linear slot rather than curving into the circular closed embrace.
Clamping down on the follower's back before count 7.
variations: Dile Que Sí with a subtle follower inside turn on 5-6-7 before settling into closed position.
notes: Often used to transition from open Casino figures back into Son or romantic Tema sections. Teachers should verify whether BOH Studios teaches the entry from standard Guapea on 1 or as a pickup on 5-6-7.

name: Doble Play
summary: A baseball-inspired Rueda partner-change call ('Double Play'): the leader leads an Enchufla on 1-3, fakes or taps at the first follower on 5-7 ('first base'), and continues to the second follower ('second base') for Dile Que No on 9-15.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 with your current follower.
Travel to the next follower on your right on 5-6-7, executing a quick hand-tap, clap, or Enchufla check ('first out') without staying.
Continue anticlockwise to the second follower on 9-11 ('second out') and complete Dile Que No with her on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn left through the initial Enchufla on 1-2-3.
Hold your perimeter spot on 5-6-7, interacting playfully with the passing leader's tap/clap without following him.
Connect with the second incoming leader on 9-11 and travel through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Stopping and doing Dile Que No with the first follower instead of continuing to the second follower.
Followers getting pulled off the perimeter by the passing leader on count 7.
variations: Doble Play with an Enchufla turn on the first passed follower before taking the second.
notes: UNSURE: Some schools execute Doble Play as two full Enchuflas with two consecutive followers before Dile Que No (3 eight-counts), while others do a 2-eight-count tap-and-pass. Verify BOH Studios' version.

name: Dos con Cuba sin Soltar (Se Fue)
spanishName: Dos con Cuba sin Soltar (Se Fue)
summary: A deceptive Rueda call that begins like 'Dame Dos con Cuba' (rhythmic 'Cu-ba' accent while retaining the current partner's hand 'sin soltar'), then suddenly releases on '¡Se fue!' to execute the actual partner change into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla or Dame initiation on 1-2-3 with the 'con Cuba' rhythmic step/clap accent on 5-6-7, keeping the left-to-right hand connection ('sin soltar') so the follower rebounds back.
Execute the rebound turn/check with the same follower on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), then on the call '¡Se fue!' release her cleanly on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) and travel counter-clockwise to the new partner.
On counts 17-24, connect with the new follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through a Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Step through the opening turn on 1-2-3 and hit the 'con Cuba' accent on 5-6-7 while maintaining a light, elastic hand connection ('sin soltar') with the leader.
Follow the rebound turn on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), then release on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) when the leader travels away on '¡Se fue!'.
On counts 17-24, receive the incoming leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: Leaders must not travel two partners away while still holding the original follower's hand ('sin soltar')—stay within arm's reach during the fake-out and only travel once the hand is released on '¡Se fue!'.
Letting go of the hand on the first eight-count before 'sin soltar' is completed.
Missing the '¡Se fue!' release cue and staying with the original partner at the end.
variations: Skipping two partners on the '¡Se fue!' exit to honour the 'Dos' in the call.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether 'Dos con Cuba sin soltar (se fue)' advances 1 partner or 2 partners when 'se fue' is triggered, and verify the exact 'con Cuba' rhythmic footwork.

name: Dos con Dos
summary: A rhythmic Rueda partner-change figure combining an Enchufla (or Dame Dos) with a synchronized two-clap percussive break before picking up the new partner in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, exchanging places with your current follower.
Release hands, step into the center/inside lane on 5-6-7 while executing two sharp rhythmic claps (usually on 7-8 or 5-6) as you travel to the next (or second) follower.
Connect with the new follower on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3 to exchange places with the leader.
Step back/in-place on 5-6-7 along the outer circle while matching the two rhythmic claps and spotting your incoming leader.
Step back on 9-11 in closed/semi-closed frame and travel through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Clapping out of sync with the caller's count.
Stopping the feet completely while clapping and arriving late to the new partner.
Confusing whether the school skips one partner or two partners on 'Dos con Dos'.
variations: Dame Dos con Dos (skipping two followers and clapping twice).
notes: UNSURE: In some Rueda systems 'Dos con Dos' means 'Dame Dos with 2 claps' (1 eight-count), while in others it is an Enchufla variation with 2 claps. Teacher should confirm BOH Studios' exact counts.

name: Dos Fly
summary: A playful baseball-themed Rueda call where leaders perform an Enchufla, clap twice overhead as if catching two high fly balls ('dos fly') while advancing down the circle, and finish with a partner change in Dile Que No.
