On 1-3, lead a check/hook turn or raise the left hand over the follower's head to reverse their turn direction, then on 5-7 bring the right hand over your own head to unwind the wrap.
Open the frame on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right under the leader's raised left arm on 1-3 into the Setenta hammerlock, keeping the right back-hand relaxed against your lower back on 5-7.
Follow the leader's overhead lead to unwind on 1-3 and pivot cleanly through the secondary turn on 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Raising the hammerlocked right hand up the follower's spine; keep the back hand at waist/hip level at all times.
Forgetting which hand goes over which head on counts 9-16.
Pulling the follower off their axis during the direction change.
variations: Finishing with an Enchufla instead of Dile Que No in Rueda.
notes: UNSURE: Numbered figures (71, 72, 75, 84, 88) vary slightly in sequence between Havana schools. Verify the exact 2nd eight-count hand sequence with Enrique before publishing.

name: Ochenta y Ocho (88)
summary: The pinnacle of the numbered Setenta/Ochenta family: a figure-8 double-hammerlock knot where both leader and follower weave through symmetrical wraps and overhead unwraps.

leaderSteps.text: Begin with a Setenta entry on 1-3 into the follower's hammerlock, then on 5-7 turn inward under the raised left arm so both partners are in a mutual double hammerlock ('88').
Rotate together around the shared axis on 1-3, then raise the right arm over the follower's head on 5-7 to unwrap her side of the knot.
Raise the left arm over your own head on 1-3 to unwrap your side, then lead a continuous hook turn or Siete check on 5-7.
Open the frame on 1-3 and finish with a clean Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right into the Setenta hammerlock on 1-3, then take tiny steps next to the leader on 5-7 as the leader wraps into the matching hammerlock.
Circle compactly with the leader on 1-3, then pivot under the raised right arm on 5-7 to release your hammerlock.
Maintain small steps on 1-3 as the leader unwraps, and follow the secondary turn on 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Stepping away from each other while both dancers are in a double hammerlock (counts 5-12); you must stay hip-to-hip with tiny steps or you will wrench both shoulders!
SAFETY: Clamping thumbs; use a frictionless two-finger hook grip.
Forgetting which hand unwraps first on counts 13-20.
variations: Entering Ochenta y Ocho from a Sombrero Doble.
notes: Strict safety rule in class: drill the double-hammerlock proximity at slow tempo first so neither partner ever feels shoulder tension.

name: Ocho para Mujeres
summary: The 'Figure-8 for Followers': an advanced Rueda figure where followers weave in a figure-8 ('ocho') path around two adjacent leaders (or leaders guide followers through a figure-8 orbit) before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla/open release on 1-3 that sends the follower into the first loop of her figure-8 orbit around you on 5-7.
Hold your station (Look and clap) on 1-3 and 5-7 as the followers weave the second loop of the figure-8 around the adjacent leader.
Collect the arriving follower on 1-3 and lead Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Start on 1-3 and trace the first loop of a figure-8 ('ocho') around your leader on 5-7.
Cross into the second loop of the figure-8 around the neighboring leader on 1-3 and 5-7 with brisk, compact steps.
Connect with the leader on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Leaders moving off their stations while followers are weaving figure-8s around them; leaders must stay anchored like pylons!
Followers taking huge loops and arriving late on count 17.
variations: Ocho (leaders trace the figure-8 around two followers).
notes: Remind leaders that in standard 'Ocho' the leaders walk the figure-8 around two followers, whereas in 'Ocho para Mujeres' the roles reverse so leaders stay anchored.

name: Ocho para Mujeres Doble
summary: An advanced Rueda figure where leaders stay stationed as posts while each follower weaves in a figure-eight ('ocho') pattern around her leader and the neighbouring leader twice ('doble'), finishing with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead the follower into an opening Enchufla/pass on 1-2-3, then hold your station in the circle on 5-6-7 while guiding the passing followers along the first loop of the figure-eight.
Maintain clear visual and hand-offer cues in place on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) to redirect the follower around the back and toward the neighbouring leader.
On counts 17-24, guide the follower through the second complete figure-eight loop ('doble') around the two leader stations on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, collect the returning (or next) follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through a clean Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Enter the weave on 1-2-3 and travel in a smooth figure-eight loop around your leader's back and toward the neighbouring leader on 5-6-7.
Loop around the neighbouring leader on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and cross back through the center of the figure-eight on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) to complete the first 'ocho'.
On counts 17-24, trace a second full figure-eight ('doble') around the two leaders on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, keeping steps small and controlled.
On counts 25-32, connect in closed frame on 1-2-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Leaders wandering out of their stations while the followers are trying to weave around them, destroying the figure-eight geometry.
Followers taking overly wide loops and running out of counts before the second 'ocho' finishes.
Collisions in the crossing lane between two leaders—followers must keep to the right of each other when passing.
variations: Ending on the neighbouring leader on count 25 to create a partner change.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether the follower finishes the second figure-eight with her original leader (no partner change) or advances to the neighbouring leader (partner change).

name: Ochosi (Orisha of the Hunt, Forest & Divine Justice)
summary: Sacred dance vocabulary of Ochosi, the master hunter, scout, and archer who embodies focus, agility, and divine justice (part of Los Guerreros alongside Eleguá and Oggún)—characterized by bow-and-arrow pantomime and alert stalking footwork.

leaderSteps.text: Step with light, agile hunter footwork on 1-3 and 5-7, scanning the forest horizon and extending the left arm forward while drawing an imaginary bowstring back to the chest with the right hand.
Release the arrow on the drum accent, leap or pivot lightly to track the quarry on 1-3, and mime slinging the game bag over the shoulder on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Move with alert, springy knee action on 1-3 and 5-7, aligning the torso diagonally to aim and draw Ochosi's bow and arrow with precision.
Execute agile directional pivots on 1-3 and 5-7, keeping the gaze sharp and focused on the target.

commonMistakes: Holding the bow-and-arrow gesture with limp wrists; Ochosi requires crisp, athletic tension across the back and shoulders as if drawing a real bow.
Looking at the floor instead of aiming toward the horizon.
variations: Crossing the index fingers to form Ochosi's bow-and-arrow emblem during Timba references to Los Guerreros.
notes: Sacred in Regla de Ocha: Ochosi's colours are cobalt/indigo blue and amber/yellow (or coral); his attributes are the bow and arrow (arco y flecha), hunting dogs, and deer antlers.

name: Oggún (Orisha of Iron, Labor & The Mountain Forest)
summary: Dedicated study of Oggún, the tireless warrior Orisha of iron, metallurgy, technology, and the deep forest ('el monte')—characterized by grounded, heavy-footed stances and rhythmic machete-clearing and blacksmith strikes.

leaderSteps.text: Sink into a wide, powerful warrior stance on 1-3 and 5-7, slashing the right arm diagonally across the body (left-to-right and right-to-left) as if clearing dense forest brush with a heavy iron machete.
Drive high-knee stomping advances and overhead blacksmith-hammer strikes on 1-3 and 5-7, engaging the lats, chest, and core on every impact.

followerSteps.text: Ground your weight deeply into the floor on 1-3 and 5-7, driving the diagonal machete-slashing arm action from your back and ribcage rather than just the wrist.
Execute strong, Earth-connected stomps and sharp chest contractions on 1-3 and 5-7, projecting Oggún's relentless strength.

commonMistakes: Swinging the machete arm loosely from the elbow without grounding the feet or engaging the torso.
SAFETY: Swinging the extended arm too wide in a crowded class or social floor; keep the diagonal machete cut within your personal frame.
variations: Wiping sweat from the brow with the forearm after a series of machete strikes.
notes: Sacred in Regla de Ocha: Oggún's colours are forest green and black (with numbers 3 and 7); his attributes are the iron cauldron (caldero), machete, anvil, hammer, and railroad spikes.

name: Oyá (Orisha of the Winds, Lightning & Transformation)
summary: Sacred dance vocabulary of Oyá, the fierce female warrior Orisha of the winds, lightning, the marketplace, and the gates of the cemetery—characterized by whirling skirt/torso spins and sweeping overhead motions with the iruke (horsetail whisk).

leaderSteps.text: Step with urgent, grounded intensity on 1-3 and 5-7, sweeping the right arm in wide overhead circles as if wielding Oyá's iruke (black horsetail whisk) to clear the air and command the wind.
Execute fast, Tornado-like traveling turns and sharp directional checks on 1-3 and 5-7, keeping the eyes fierce and focused and the chest proud.

followerSteps.text: Grip the skirt with one hand (whipping it like a rising storm wind) while whirling the other arm overhead with the imaginary iruke on 1-3 and 5-7.
Spin rapidly like a whirlwind on 1-3 and hit sharp, lightning-bolt torso contractions and warrior checks on 5-7.

commonMistakes: Dancing Oyá with soft, coy coquetry (like Ochún) instead of embodying her fierce, commanding tempest energy.
Spinning without spotting or grounding through the feet.
variations: Incorporating Oyá's overhead iruke wind-sweep during high-intensity Timba horn climaxes.
notes: Sacred in Regla de Ocha (Santería): Oyá's colours are burgundy/wine red and nine distinct colours (representing the number 9); her attributes are the iruke (horsetail whisk), copper crown, and machete/centella (lightning). Always teach and dance with deep cultural respect.

name: Panqué
summary: The 'Cupcake / Pancake Flip': a quick, playful Rueda turn or partner-switch figure featuring a rapid wrist/hand flip and an accent clap or check before resuming Guapea or Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea, lead a quick inward/upward hand flip on 1-2-3 to turn the follower (or exchange places) like flipping a pancake.
Catch/check the frame cleanly on 5-6-7 (or complete Dile Que No with the current/next partner per house rule).

followerSteps.text: Respond to the crisp upward lead on 1-2-3 with a compact, balanced turn on the balls of your feet.
Settle back into frame on 5-6-7 with a clean check or Dile Que No.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Flipping or jerking the follower's wrist forcefully; the 'flip' is a visual cue, led smoothly with a soft two-finger hook.
Over-spinning on count 3.
variations: Panqué Doble.
notes: UNSURE: 'Panqué' has very different regional meanings (in some schools a quick Enchufla-style hand flip, in others a clap/hip pat). Teacher must verify BOH Studios' version.

name: Parte el Brazo
summary: Colloquially 'Fold the Arm': an intermediate Setenta/hammerlock Rueda figure where the follower's arm is guided into a clean, tension-free waist-level hammerlock fold before unwrapping into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a two-hand turn on 1-2-3 into a compact hammerlock fold ('parte el brazo'), keeping the lower hand strictly at the follower's hip/waist level.
Lead an overhead unwrap turn with the top hand on 5-6-7 while releasing the lower hand smoothly.
Collect the follower (or next follower) on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn into the hammerlock on 1-2-3, resting the back of your wrist/forearm softly against your lower back with zero shoulder tension.
Unwind under the raised top arm on 5-6-7 on your own vertical axis.
Step back on 9-11 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Never take the name 'Parte el brazo' ('break the arm') literally! Raising the hammerlock hand above waist level or pulling backward can injure the rotator cuff.
Standing too far from the follower during the hammerlock.
variations: Parte el Brazo Doble (both partners in a hammerlock).
notes: Always preface this move in class with a strict shoulder-safety reminder: soft elbows, loose two-finger hook, and waist-level back hand.

name: Paséala Caminando
summary: A travelling Rueda call where couples walk together in Paséala formation around the perimeter of the circle, maintaining continuous circular progression before closing with Dile Que No (or changing partners if called).

leaderSteps.text: Connect in semi-closed Paséala hold on 1-2-3 and walk forward along the Rueda circumference alongside the follower on 5-6-7, matching the group's stride length.
Check the forward progression on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) with an Exhíbela or frame pivot, and lead the follower through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Step into the Paséala promenade walk on 1-2-3 and continue walking gracefully along the circle on 5-6-7 with Cuban hip movement and upright posture.
Turn or pivot on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) as the leader checks the walk, and step through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Walking on every beat (1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8) instead of preserving the Cuban 1-2-3 (pause 4), 5-6-7 (pause 8) cadence.
Overtaking the couple in front and distorting the spacing of the circle.
Leaders leaning forward at the waist while walking.
variations: Paséala caminando con alarde (adding synchronized arm styling on counts 4 and 8).
notes: UNSURE: In some Rueda circles, 'Paséala caminando' keeps the same partner while rotating the whole wheel, whereas in others the followers walk past the leaders to effect a partner change. Confirm whether a partner change occurs in your curriculum.

name: Paséala para Abajo
summary: A Rueda call where the leader guides the follower in a circular Paseo walk backward ('down the line' clockwise) on the first eight-count before bringing her back across in a Dile Que No without changing partners.

leaderSteps.text: From closed hold or after Dile Que No, step in a tight pivot at the center of the couple's axis on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7 while guiding the follower in a smooth clockwise circular walk around the outside.
Check the backward circular momentum gently on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), open the frame, and lead the follower forward across the slot in a Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) to resume Guapea.

followerSteps.text: Walk smoothly along the circular circumference on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, keeping the torso connected to the leader's right arm or hand while travelling clockwise ('para abajo').
Step back-side-together on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) as the leader redirects the energy, then travel forward in a standard Dile Que No arc on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) to face the same partner.

commonMistakes: Followers rushing or taking overly large steps on 1-8, pulling the leader off his central axis.
Leaders using arm strength to drag the follower around rather than rotating their own ribcage and hips.
Confusing 'para abajo' (clockwise/backward along the Rueda line of dance) with 'para arriba' (counter-clockwise).
variations: Adding a follower turn (Exhíbela) on counts 9-11 before the final Dile Que No.
Finishing with a Dame on counts 13-15 if the caller shouts 'y dame' at the end.
notes: UNSURE: Depending on the Rueda school, 'Paséala para abajo' can mean walking the follower backward in closed/semi-closed paseo around the couple's axis, or passing the follower to the previous leader ('abajo' in the Rueda). Verify whether your curriculum keeps the same partner or results in a backward partner change.

name: Paséala por Abajo
summary: A circular Rueda figure where the leader guides the follower in a Paséala trajectory combined with a duck-under ('por abajo') or low circular pass before finishing with Dile Que No (or changing partners).

leaderSteps.text: Lead the follower into a circular Paséala walk on 1-2-3, then raise the connected arm on 5-6-7 to duck underneath ('por abajo') while keeping the circular flow alive.
Emerge from the duck-under on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) to lead an Exhíbela check (or advance along the circle), and finish with Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Walk smoothly around the leader in the Paséala arc on 1-2-3, keeping the connected arm rounded overhead on 5-6-7 as the leader passes underneath.
Complete the turn/check on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and travel cleanly across the slot in a Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Safety: Whoever ducks 'por abajo' must bend at the knees and keep the head and chest upright rather than hinging at the waist, never pulling down on the partner's arm.
Stopping the circular Paseo momentum when preparing the duck-under.
Confusing 'por abajo' (underneath the arm / low level) with 'para abajo' (direction down the Rueda line).
variations: Follower ducking under the leader's arm ('por abajo') during the Paseo walk.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether 'Paséala por abajo' in your curriculum means ducking under the arm bridge during Paséala, dancing the Paséala in a low bent-knee crouch ('por el piso / por abajo'), or passing the follower down the circle (partner change).

name: Paséala por Arriba
summary: An elevated variation of Paséala where the leader guides the follower in a sweeping circular walk while maintaining an overhead arm arch and continuous rotational flow.

leaderSteps.text: From Guapea or closed hold, open the frame on 1-3 and raise the connected arm to create a continuous overhead arch.
Walk forward/clockwise (por arriba) around the circle on 5-6-7 while guiding the follower along the outer arc.
Lead a smooth outside turn under the arch on 9-11 and resolve with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Begin the circular Paseo walk on 1-3, connecting through a light overhead finger hook.
Glide forward around the circle on 5-6-7, using your free hand to style the skirt ('con falda') or ribcage.
Turn cleanly under the raised arch on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Holding the raised arm completely straight and locked, which tires the follower's shoulder.
Walking in a flat line instead of curving around a shared center point.
Rushing the walk at fast tempos.
variations: Alternating Paséala por Arriba (1-8) with Paséala por Abajo (9-16).
notes: Keep the overhead arch soft and slightly in front of the follower's forehead line, never behind their head.

name: Paséala por Bayamo
summary: A flowing combination that merges the circular Paseo walk of Paséala with the sweeping overhead wrap and turn of Bayamo before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate a smooth circular Paséala walk with the follower on 1-3 and 5-7 around the shared orbit.
Transition seamlessly into the Bayamo wrap and sweeping circular turn on 1-3 and 5-7.
Collect the follower in semi-closed frame on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Glide through the circular Paséala walk on 1-3 and 5-7 with expressive free-arm/skirt styling.
Follow the sweeping Bayamo turn and wrap on 1-3 and 5-7 while maintaining your circular trajectory.
Step back on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: Breaking the smooth circular walking momentum with a jerky transition on count 9.
Flattening the circle into a linear slot.
variations: Paséala por Bayamo y Dame (changing partners at the end).
notes: Connects the Improver 'paseala' and Intermediate 'coca-cola-y-bayamo' curriculum modules.

name: Paséala y al Revés
summary: A circular Rueda figure where the couple walks through a standard Paséala arc in one direction on the first eight-count, reverses the circular trajectory ('al revés') on the second eight-count, and finishes with Exhíbela and Dile Que No without changing partners.

leaderSteps.text: Lead the follower into a circular Paséala walk forward/counter-clockwise around your right side on 1-2-3, checking gently on 5-6-7 while pivoting in the center.
Redirect the frame smoothly on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) to guide the follower in the opposite circular direction ('al revés', clockwise) around your axis through 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, lead the follower through an Exhíbela turn on 1-2-3 and finish with a standard Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Walk smoothly in the circular Paséala trajectory on 1-2-3 and prepare for the direction check on 5-6-7 while maintaining frame connection.
Pivot cleanly on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) as the leader reverses the lead, walking around the arc in the opposite direction on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, execute the Exhíbela right turn on 1-2-3 and travel across in Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Jerking the follower's shoulder or hand on count 8/9 to reverse her direction instead of absorbing her momentum with the core.
Stepping in straight lines instead of maintaining a continuous circular arc around the couple's center.
Drifting into neighbouring couples' stations during the reverse walk.
variations: Finishing with 'y dame' on counts 21-23 to change partners at the end.
notes: Focus on smooth deceleration at the end of the first eight-count so the reversal ('al revés') feels effortless for the follower.

name: Paseo
summary: A relaxed, circular walking figure where the leader and follower stroll around the perimeter of their shared circle—essential for lyrical Tema intros and breathing between complex turn combinations.

leaderSteps.text: From open or one-hand connection, curve forward-and-around the circle on left (1), right (2), left (3) with smooth, unhurried weight transfers.
Continue walking around the circular arc on right (5), left (6), right (7), or pivot to face your partner to resume Guapea.

followerSteps.text: Walk smoothly around the opposite side of the circle (or alongside the leader) on right (1), left (2), right (3) with natural Cuban hip motion.
Continue the circular stroll on left (5), right (6), left (7), styling your free hand and reconnecting frame on 7.

commonMistakes: Walking with stiff, robotic knees instead of a smooth Cuban stride.
Dragging the partner forward with the arm instead of walking with your own center of mass.
Breaking the circular floor craft and bumping into neighboring couples.
variations: Paséala por Abajo (leader guides follower's walk while backing up around the circle).
Paseo en Son (stepping contratiempo on 2-3-4, 6-7-8).
notes: Connects directly to the existing 'paseala' curriculum move; this entry isolates the foundational Paseo walking mechanics.

name: Paso Cruzado (Cross Step)
summary: A dynamic solo Suelta step where the active foot crosses cleanly in front of (or behind) the standing leg on counts 1 and 5, creating natural torso twist and hip articulation.

leaderSteps.text: Cross left foot diagonally in front of right foot on 1, rock weight back onto right foot on 2, and step left foot out to the left side on 3.
Cross right foot diagonally in front of left foot on 5, rock weight back onto left foot on 6, and step right foot out to the right side on 7.

followerSteps.text: Cross right foot diagonally in front of left foot on 1 (or left in solo warmup), rock back on 2, and open to the side on 3 while keeping shoulders facing forward.
Cross the opposite foot in front on 5, rock weight on 6, and open to the side on 7 with fluid hip rotation.

commonMistakes: Turning the whole chest sideways on the cross step instead of letting the lower body twist against a stable upper frame.
Tripping over your own shin by crossing too deeply.
variations: Paso Cruzado por Atrás (crossing behind on counts 1 and 5, which is Paso de Cumbia).
notes: Great for building dissociation between the pelvis and the ribcage.

name: Paso de Cumbia
summary: A rotational back-cross basic where the working foot hooks diagonally behind the standing leg on counts 1 and 5, opening the hips and chest from side to side.

leaderSteps.text: Step left foot diagonally behind right foot on 1 (opening torso slightly left), rock weight onto right foot in place on 2, and step left foot to the left side on 3.
Step right foot diagonally behind left foot on 5 (opening torso slightly right), rock weight onto left foot in place on 6, and step right foot to the right side on 7.

followerSteps.text: Step right foot diagonally behind left foot on 1, rock onto left foot in place on 2, and return right foot to the side on 3 with a natural hip figure-8.
Step left foot diagonally behind right foot on 5, rock onto right foot in place on 6, and return left foot to the side on 7.

commonMistakes: Leaning weight far backward on counts 1 and 5 instead of keeping the back-cross compact under the center of mass.
Forgetting to return to neutral center on counts 3 and 7.
variations: Adding a syncopated tap on 4 and 8 before crossing behind.
notes: Also used inside partnerwork during Guapea and Exhíbela variations.

name: Paso de Son (Solo)
summary: The foundational solo basic of Cuban Son danced with elegant upright carriage, stepping side-to-side or in a compact box while accenting the contratiempo pulse.

leaderSteps.text: Hold or gently tap on count 1, step left foot to the left side on 2, and close or shift weight onto right foot on 3 while settling the left hip.
Hold or gently tap on count 5, step right foot to the right side on 6, and close or shift weight onto left foot on 7 with poised torso carriage.

followerSteps.text: Hold or tap on count 1, step right foot to the right side on 2, and draw left foot to meet it on 3 with soft figure-8 hip motion.
Hold or tap on count 5, step left foot to the left side on 6, and draw right foot together on 7 while keeping elbows softly framed.

commonMistakes: Stepping heavily on counts 1 and 5 when practicing traditional contratiempo Son phrasing.
Bouncing vertically with the head instead of gliding smoothly across the floor.
Dropping the chest and looking down at the feet.
variations: Dancing Paso de Son A Tiempo (stepping on 1-2-3, 5-6-7) for beginner transition drills before switching to contratiempo (2-3-4, 6-7-8).
notes: In strict Son Cubano, steps fall on 2-3-4 (pause 1) and 6-7-8 (pause 5); under our Casino count-grouping rules, teachers can drill both A Tiempo (1-3, 5-7) and Contratiempo emphasis.

name: Patín
summary: The 'Skate / Scooter': after an Enchufla, the leaders slide/skate across the center of the circle with a playful scooting motion to pick up a new partner into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a clean Enchufla on 1-2-3 and release connection.
Glide forward toward the next follower (or across the circle) on 5-6-7 using a smooth 'skating' or scooter push-and-glide footwork motion.
Connect with the new follower on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Complete the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Dance a playful skating/sliding basic in place along the perimeter on 5-6-7 while spotting the incoming leader.
Step back on 9-11 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Sliding recklessly on a slick wooden floor and losing balance; keep your center of gravity over your standing leg.
Arriving late to the new follower on count 9.
variations: Patineta (skateboard variation in Improver level).
notes: UNSURE: In some Rueda circles, 'Patín' crosses to the opposite side of the circle (like Cruce), while in others it moves one partner anticlockwise. Verify with Enrique.

name: Patín con Bamboleo
summary: A Rueda combination pairing the center skating slide of Patín with a deep circular thoracic/hip sway ('con bamboleo') before advancing to the next partner in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, release the follower, and step into the center of the circle on 5-6-7 with the lateral Patín skating slide.
Plant the feet in a wide grounded stance in the center on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) to execute a full circular 'bamboleo' torso and hip sway.
On counts 17-24, exit the center counter-clockwise toward the next follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the opening Enchufla on 1-2-3, then mark basic steps or match the skating slide along the outer perimeter on 5-6-7.
Match the grounded circular 'bamboleo' body sway and ribcage roll on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) on the outer ring.
On counts 17-24, connect with the incoming leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: Support the lower back with core engagement during the deep 'bamboleo' sway, and keep knees soft during the skating slide.
Rushing out of the Bamboleo groove before count 17.
Performing the Bamboleo only from the neck instead of engaging the ribcage and pelvis.
variations: Adding synchronized overhead arm waves during the Bamboleo on counts 9-15.
notes: Great call to hit during a heavy timba montuno or mambo groove (especially songs by Bamboleo).

name: Patín Doble
summary: An extended Rueda figure where leaders step into the center for two rounds of 'skating' slide steps (Patín) before picking up a new partner and exiting with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, release the follower, and step into the center of the circle on 5-6-7 to begin the first skating slide motion.
Perform a full eight-count of rhythmic skating/sliding steps ('patín') in the center on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15), shifting weight smoothly side-to-side.
On counts 17-24, exit the center toward the next designated follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through a Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the opening Enchufla on 1-2-3, then mark basic steps in place along the outside ring on 5-6-7.
Maintain the outer circle by dancing Cuban basic or matching skating slides in place on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) while the leaders perform Patín in the center.
On counts 17-24, connect with the incoming leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: Over-extending the lateral slide on a sticky or slippery dance floor, which can strain the groin or knee—keep the slide controlled under the hips.
Leaders losing spatial orientation in the center and returning to the wrong follower.
Coming out of the center one eight-count too early (doing regular Patín instead of Patín Doble).
variations: Followers joining the skating motion on the outside ring.
notes: UNSURE: In some schools, 'Patín Doble' means two Enchuflas with two skating slides back-to-back, while in others it doubles the duration of the skating groove in the center. Confirm which version is taught.

name: Patín Pa' Arriba
summary: A variation of the Patín Rueda call where leaders perform the center skating slide after an Enchufla, then exit upstream ('pa' arriba', clockwise) to change partners with the previous follower in the circle.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, release the follower, and step into the center of the circle on 5-6-7 with the lateral skating slide ('patín').
Complete the second skating slide on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) while angling clockwise ('pa' arriba') toward the previous follower, and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the Enchufla on 1-2-3, then mark basic steps in place along the outer ring on 5-6-7.
Mark in place on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) while looking to your right (downstream) to receive the leader coming 'pa' arriba', and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Safety: Keep the lateral skating slide controlled with bent knees so you do not slip or collide with leaders in the center.
Exiting counter-clockwise (normal Dame direction) out of habit instead of going clockwise ('pa' arriba').
Followers looking to their left for the new leader when he is actually arriving from their right.
variations: Continuous Patín pa' arriba walking groove around the circle.
notes: In Cuban Rueda terminology, moving counter-clockwise (standard Dame) is going 'abajo', while moving clockwise to the previous partner is going 'arriba'.

name: Patineta
summary: The 'Skateboard': an upgrade to Patín where, after an Enchufla on 1-3, dancers turn sideways and mime pushing a skateboard along the circle on 5-7 before picking up the next follower in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Enchufla on 1-2-3 and release connection.
Angle your torso sideways like riding a skateboard and push-glide on 5-6-7 along the inside lane toward the next follower.
Connect with the new follower on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Complete the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Mime the playful sideways skateboard push-and-balance in place on the outer circle on 5-6-7.
Receive the incoming leader on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Kicking the pushing leg too far back and clipping the dancer behind you.
Losing the 5-6-7 count while acting out the skateboard motion.
variations: Adding a small hop ('ollie') on count 7 before stepping onto count 9.
notes: Confirm with Enrique whether Patineta moves 1 partner anticlockwise or crosses the circle.

name: Patineta con Bamboleo
summary: A playful Rueda variation where dancers mimic pushing a skateboard ('patineta') after an Enchufla, transition into a deep circular 'bamboleo' body sway, and change partners into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, then pivot sideways on 5-6-7 with one foot planted on the 'board' and the free foot pushing the floor twice like riding a skateboard ('patineta').
Settle into a wide grounded stance on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) to perform the sweeping circular 'bamboleo' torso and hip sway.
On counts 17-24, travel to the next follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through a Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the opening Enchufla on 1-2-3, then perform the matching 'patineta' skateboard push in place along the circle on 5-6-7.
Execute the full circular 'bamboleo' ribcage and hip roll on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, connect with the arriving leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Confusing 'Patín' (side-to-side roller/ice skating slide) with 'Patineta' (single-leg skateboard push).
Losing balance on the standing leg during the skateboard push on 5-6-7.
Forgetting to advance to the new partner on count 17.
variations: Using the 'patineta' push to actually travel counter-clockwise around the inside of the circle.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether both leaders and followers perform the 'patineta' skateboard motion in your school, or if followers join the center for this call.

name: Patineta Doble
summary: An extended Rueda call where dancers perform an Enchufla followed by two full sets of 'patineta' (skateboard-push) shines before advancing to the next partner in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, release the follower, and perform the first set of 'patineta' skateboard pushes toward the center on 5-6-7.
Execute a second full eight-count of 'patineta' pushes (switching sides or travelling along the inner ring) on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, connect with the next follower on 1-2-3 and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the Enchufla on 1-2-3, then perform or mark the first 'patineta' phrase along the outer ring on 5-6-7.
Continue with the second 'patineta' phrase in place on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, receive the incoming leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Locking the standing knee during the repeated skateboard pushes, which fatigues the hip and looks rigid.
Exiting to Dile Que No on count 9 instead of completing the 'doble' repetition.
Drifting too far across the center and losing the target partner.
variations: Doing an Enchufla between the first and second Patineta.
notes: Level note: Rueda.Casino lists it as Advanced; mechanics are similar to Patín Doble, so focus on crisp syncopation and weight control on the standing leg.

name: Pedro Navaja
summary: Inspired by Rubén Blades' iconic character *Pedro Navaja* ('hands always in his coat pockets'): an advanced Rueda figure where leaders tuck one or both hands into their pockets (or behind their back) and lead/orbit using pure torso and shoulder framing before Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-3, then slip your hands into your pockets (or behind your back) on 5-7 while adopting Pedro Navaja's cool, low-slung street swagger.
Circle and interact with the follower (or travel to the next follower) on 1-3 and 5-7 using shoulder/torso framing and eye contact with hands in pockets.
Bring your hands out on 1-3 to collect the follower and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left through the Enchufla on 1-3 and match the playful street-swagger groove on 5-7.
Circle and play off the leader's torso/shoulder lead on 1-3 and 5-7 with expressive Cuban hip and shoulder styling.
Connect on 1-3 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Keep your hands ready to slip out of your pockets instantly on count 17 so you never trip or lose balance.
Slouching stiffly instead of keeping a rhythmic Cuban bounce.
variations: Pedro Navaja leading a shoulder-check turn without hands.
notes: Directly references the famous lyric from *Pedro Navaja*: 'Las manos siempre dentro del gabán' (hands always inside the coat pockets).

name: Pelota (Una, Dos, Tres)
summary: A rhythmic Rueda partner-change series where an Enchufla on 1-3 is followed by 1, 2, or 3 synchronized claps on counts 5-7 before picking up the next follower in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Enchufla on 1-2-3, trading places with your current follower.
Turn toward the inside lane on 5-6-7 and clap once on 7 (Pelota Una), twice on 7-8 (Pelota Dos), or three times on 7-and-8 (Pelota Tres) while advancing to the next follower.
Collect the new follower on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Step in place on the outer circle on 5-6-7 and execute the called number of claps (1, 2, or 3) on counts 7-8.
Connect with the incoming leader on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Clapping on count 5 instead of waiting for the musical accent on 7 / 7-8 (check house timing).
Drifting out of the circle formation while clapping.
variations: Pelota Cuatro (four rapid claps).
notes: Confirm whether BOH Studios claps on counts 5, 5-6, 5-6-7 or on counts 7, 7-8, 7-and-8.

name: Pelota Hasta Cinco
summary: A progressive Rueda clapping sequence after an Enchufla that counts claps from one all the way up to five across consecutive phrases, finishing with a partner change into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 to swap places and face the center, then begin the progressive clap sequence starting with 1 clap on the first pause/phrase and 2 claps on the next.
Continue marking basic footwork in place while executing the 3-clap and 4-clap rhythmic patterns in unison with the circle.
On the final phrase, execute the 5-clap syncopated burst ('uno-dos-tres-cuatro-cinco'), advance to the next follower on the right, and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the Enchufla on 1-2-3, then mark basic footwork along the circle while executing the 1-clap and 2-clap phrases.
Maintain the basic step in place while performing the 3-clap and 4-clap sequences with Cuban hip motion.
Complete the 5-clap burst, connect with the incoming leader from the left, and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Stopping the feet while concentrating on the 4-clap and 5-clap rhythms.
Speeding up the claps so they fall off the clave/tumbao pulse.
Moving to the new partner before the 5-clap sequence is finished.
variations: Doing an Enchufla swap between every single number (1 through 5) instead of staying in the center until 5.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether your teachers perform an Enchufla before every number (which takes 6 to 10 eight-counts) or hold the center after one Enchufla and count the claps 1-2-3-4-5 across 3 to 4 eight-counts.

name: Pelota Loca
summary: The 'Crazy Ball': an energetic upgrade to Pelota where an Enchufla on 1-3 is followed by a flurry of rapid, syncopated claps, turns, or multi-partner passes on 5-7 before picking up the next follower in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a crisp Enchufla on 1-2-3 and release connection.
Execute the 'Pelota Loca' rhythmic flurry (rapid claps overhead/low plus a quick spin or skip-pass) on 5-6-7 while advancing along the circle.
Connect with the incoming follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn left through the Enchufla on 1-2-3.
Match the 'Pelota Loca' rapid claps and solo turn in place on the outer perimeter on 5-6-7.
Step back on 9-11 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Losing spatial control during the fast claps/spin and bumping into the next couple.
Missing the count 9 pickup.
variations: Extended 3-bar Pelota Loca.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm the exact clap/turn rhythm BOH Studios uses for Pelota Loca.

name: Pelota Moderna
summary: A stylized contemporary variation of the Pelota Rueda call combining an Enchufla with syncopated body/chest taps or modern timba footwork accents before advancing to the next partner in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 to face the center, then execute the modern syncopated clap/chest-hit and footwork groove on 5-6-7.
Complete the rhythmic break on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) while travelling counter-clockwise to the next follower, and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the Enchufla on 1-2-3, then perform the matching syncopated clap and body-percussion pattern in place on 5-6-7.
Finish the groove on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), connect with the incoming leader on count 12, and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Doing standard Pelota claps instead of the stylized modern pattern.
Losing the beat 1 timing after the syncopated hits on counts 9-11.
Arriving late to the new follower on count 12.
variations: Adding a low Squat/Despelote groove on counts 9-11.
notes: UNSURE: 'Pelota Moderna' is a stylized call whose exact clap/tap rhythm differs between instructors. Teacher should verify the exact counts 5-11 choreography.

name: Por Mí, Por Ti
summary: 'For Me, For You': an alternating Rueda figure where the leader first ducks/turns for himself ('por mí') on 1-3, then turns the follower ('por ti') on 5-7 before resolving or switching partners into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: On 1-2-3 ('por mí'), execute an inside/underarm turn or duck-under for yourself while keeping connection.
On 5-6-7 ('por ti'), immediately raise the arm to lead a matching turn for the follower while stepping toward the next station.
Collect the follower on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Frame the leader's turn on 1-2-3 ('por mí') while maintaining your circular basic.
Execute your underarm turn on 5-6-7 ('por ti') on the perimeter.
Step back on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the order and turning the follower on 1-3 when 'Por mí' comes first.
SAFETY: Pulling the arm down during the leader's turn on 1-3.
variations: Por Ti, Por Mí (reversing the turn order).
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios teaches 'Por mí, por ti' as alternating turns or a specific clap/tap pattern.

name: Preciosa
summary: A flowing, display-oriented Casino figure where the leader frames the follower in a cuddle/sweetheart or shoulder-presentation wrap before opening out smoothly.

leaderSteps.text: From a two-hand hold, lead the follower into a right turn on 1-3, wrapping them gently in front or to your right side in a sweetheart presentation.
Walk together in a shared circular arc on 5-6-7, letting the follower's posture shine.
Unwrap the follower with a smooth outside turn on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn right on 1-3 into the sweetheart wrap, keeping your forearms resting lightly over your own chest/frame.
Walk with the leader around the circle on 5-6-7 with proud chest posture and head styling.
Unwind cleanly on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling the follower's arms backward behind their shoulder line in the wrap.
Rushing through the presentation walk on 5-7 instead of letting the figure breathe.
Collapsing the upper back.
variations: Adding a pause and head-turn accent on count 7 when a horn hit lands.
notes: UNSURE: 'Preciosa' is taught differently across schools (sometimes as a sweetheart wrap, sometimes as a variation of Sombrero/Evelyn). Teacher should verify exact handwork.

name: Prima con la Hermana
summary: An extension of Prima (Adiós) where the leader executes the initial Prima pass on 1-3, then steps across on 5-7 to greet/embrace the next follower ('the sister') before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Prima (Adiós) on 1-2-3: step across in front of your follower while ducking/passing under your raised left arm.
Release the first follower and step toward the next follower ('la hermana') on 5-6-7, greeting her with an Enchufla-style check or embrace.
Complete the transition with the new follower (or return, depending on call) on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Step forward/in-place on 1-2-3 as the leader passes across in front of you for Prima.
Pivot to face the inside of the circle on 5-6-7 and greet the incoming leader arriving from your left.
Step back on 9-11 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Ducking under the Prima arm with a bent neck instead of lowering with the knees.
Pulling on the first follower's left hand while already stepping toward the second follower on count 4.
variations: Prima con la Hermana y Toda la Familia.
notes: UNSURE: In some Rueda schools, 'Prima con la Hermana' stays with the original partner after an Enchufla, while in others it changes partner to 'the sister' (the next follower). Verify BOH Studios' rule.

name: Prima con la Vecina
summary: A Rueda call where the leader executes a Prima (Adiós) check with his current partner on counts 1-3, then pivots to perform an Enchufla/greeting pass with the neighbouring follower ('la vecina') before changing partners in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Step into the Prima check with your current partner on 1-2-3, raising the left arm as you pass under on 5-6-7, and immediately orient toward the neighbouring follower.
Lead an Enchufla or check with the neighbouring follower on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and finish by leading the designated new partner through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Step into the Prima check on 1-2-3 and pivot on 5-6-7 as the leader passes under his arm.
Execute the Enchufla/turn with the neighbouring leader on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), connect in closed frame on count 12, and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Safety: Leaders must bend their knees and keep their chest upright when ducking under their own arm during the Prima on counts 5-7.
Confusing 'Prima con la hermana' and 'Prima con la vecina'—listen carefully to whether the school turns the current follower first or goes straight to the neighbour.
Pulling the neighbour off the circle perimeter on counts 9-11.
variations: Prima con la vecina y quédate (staying with the neighbour at the end).
notes: UNSURE: Depending on the Rueda lineage, 'Prima con la vecina' either starts with Prima on your own partner and then interacts with the next woman, or initiates Prima directly with the woman on the left ('la vecina'). Confirm exact choreography.

name: Prima Doble
summary: An extended variation of Prima (Adiós) where the leader executes the initial Prima pass on 1-3, rebounds or hooks back on 5-7 for a second pass, and resolves with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Prima (Adiós) on 1-2-3, crossing in front of the follower while passing under your raised left arm.
Check the momentum on 5 and lead a second consecutive pass/turn across on 5-6-7 while keeping the left-to-right hand connection soft.
Open into semi-closed hold on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Step forward/in-place on 1-2-3 as the leader crosses in front of you for the first Prima.
Feel the check on 5 and pivot smoothly through the second Prima exchange on 5-6-7.
Step back on 9-11 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Ducking by bending the neck forward instead of lowering with the knees on both underarm passes.
Jerking the follower's left arm on the count 5 rebound check.
variations: Prima Doble con Dame (switching to the next follower on the exit).
notes: Great preparation before attempting the Advanced 'Adiós Doble' partner-change figure.

name: Prima y Quédate
summary: A Rueda call where the couple performs a Prima (Adiós) on counts 1-3, and upon the call '¡y quédate!' the leader cancels the partner change and keeps the same partner by leading Dile Que No on 5-7.

leaderSteps.text: Step forward into the closed Prima check on 1-2, then raise the left arm on 3 to duck underneath while turning clockwise to face the partner. Pause on 4.
Instead of releasing and moving to the next partner (as when Prima is used as 'Adiós' in some Ruedas), stay connected with the current follower and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7. Pause on 8.

followerSteps.text: Step back-side-together in the Prima check on 1-2-3 while keeping the right arm softly rounded as the leader ducks under. Pause on 4.
Remain with the same leader, connecting into his right arm on count 4, and travel across in a standard Dile Que No on 5-6-7. Pause on 8.

commonMistakes: Safety: Leaders pulling down on the follower's right arm while ducking under on count 3-4—maintain your own posture and bend at the knees.
Releasing the left-to-right hand hold on count 4 out of habit.
Rushing the duck-under on count 2 before completing the forward check.
variations: 2-eight-count version ('Prima con la hermana y quédate') where the leader adds the right-hand Enchufla on 5-7 and closes with Dile Que No on 9-15.
notes: In Rueda lineages where 'Adiós / Prima' normally changes partner, 'Prima y quédate' cancels the change. In lineages where bare 'Prima' already keeps the partner, 'Prima y quédate' often refers to cancelling the partner change at the end of 'Prima con la hermana'.

name: Príncipe Bueno / Príncipe Malo
summary: 'Good Prince / Bad Prince': after an Enchufla on 1-3, the leader greets the next follower either as 'Príncipe Bueno' (gallantly kissing her hand on 5-7) or 'Príncipe Malo' (playfully faking/snubbing or wagging a finger on 5-7) before Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 and release your current partner.

Step to the next follower on 5-6-7: for 'Príncipe Bueno', bow slightly and kiss the back of her hand (or your own thumb on her hand); for 'Príncipe Malo', strike a cheeky attitude pose or fake the kiss.
Collect the new follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Complete the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Present your hand royally on 5-6-7 for 'Príncipe Bueno', or react with playful indignation/sass for 'Príncipe Malo'.
Step back on 9-11 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling the follower's hand roughly toward your face; bring your own thumb to your lips while holding her hand gently at chest height.
Taking too long with the theatrical acting and missing count 9.
variations: In some schools, 'Príncipe Malo' skips the kissed follower and moves to the next follower on 9-15.
notes: UNSURE: Verify whether BOH Studios keeps the greeted follower on 'Príncipe Malo' or skips her to take the next one.

name: Puente Doble
summary: The 'Double Bridge': an advanced figure where both dancers pass underneath high two-hand arm bridges in alternating sequence while rotating around their shared center.

leaderSteps.text: From a two-hand hold, raise both arms to form the first high bridge on 1-3, ducking/passing underneath while guiding the follower around on 5-7.
Maintain the two-hand connection and form the second bridge on 1-3, guiding the follower underneath the arch on 5-7 while you counter-rotate.
Unwind the crossed arms overhead on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Walk around the leader on 1-3 and 5-7 while holding your arms in a stable, high bridge arch as the leader passes underneath.
Pass smoothly underneath the second two-hand bridge on 1-3 and 5-7 by bending your knees slightly and keeping your spine tall.
Turn cleanly out of the unwrap on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling down on the partner's wrists while ducking under the bridge; the person ducking must lower their own body weight with their legs.
SAFETY: Clamping thumbs during the 180-degree wrist rotations under the bridge.
Collapsing the bridge arch too early on count 6.
variations: Executing Puente Doble in Rueda de Casino with a partner switch on the final Dile Que No.
notes: Because I am 194 cm tall, duck-under bridges like Puente Doble require deep knee flexion (squat mechanics) rather than rounding the upper back—great teaching point for taller leaders!

name: Quédatela
summary: 'Keep Her!': a modifier call shouted mid-Enchufla or mid-combination that instructs leaders NOT to switch to the next follower, keeping their current partner for Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead the called entry figure (such as Enchufla) on 1-2-3.
When the caller shouts '¡Quédatela!', stay with your current follower on 5-6-7 (often wrapping her into closed hold) instead of advancing to the next station.
Lead Dile Que No with your original follower on 9-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the 1-2-3 entry turn.
On the '¡Quédatela!' call, keep your visual focus and frame with your current leader on 5-6-7.
Walk cleanly through Dile Que No with your original leader on 9-15.

commonMistakes: Walking away to the next follower on autopilot and leaving your partner stranded.
Yanking the follower back if you realized the call late.
variations: Enchufla Doble y Quédatela.
notes: Essential Rueda listening drill so leaders don't automatically switch partners on every Enchufla.

name: La Reina
summary: The 'Queen': a showpiece advanced figure designed to crown and showcase the follower with an overhead tiara/crown arm framing, continuous circular walks, and a flourish exit.

leaderSteps.text: Enter with a two-hand turn on 1-3 that wraps the follower into a regal presentation frame on 5-7, with the joined hands framing above/around her head like a crown.
Promenade the follower around the circle on 1-3 and 5-7, giving her space to style while you maintain a supportive, tension-free frame.
Release the crown wrap into a spinning outside turn on 1-3 and close with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn cleanly into the presentation wrap on 1-3 and settle into the 'Reina' crown frame on 5-7 with lifted chest and proud posture.
Glide around the circle on 1-3 and 5-7, accentuating the music with Cuban hip action and expressive head/shoulder styling.
Spot cleanly through the exit turn on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Resting the 'crown' hands on the follower's head or pressing down on her neck/shoulders.
Rushing the presentation promenade like a race instead of letting the follower shine.
Over-leading the exit turn.
variations: Adding a musical freeze (bloque) on count 15 when a horn hit lands.
notes: UNSURE: 'La Reina' has multiple choreographed variations across Cuban schools. Teacher should confirm BOH Studios' exact hand-hold sequence.

name: Reparto Basic Step
summary: The foundational street groove of modern Havana Cuban urban music (Reparto / Cubatón): a low-center, knees-bent polyrhythmic step combining ankle/heel pivots, pelvic locks, and relaxed street swagger.

leaderSteps.text: Drop into a wide, low athletic stance and step/bounce on 1-2-3 while swiveling the heels inward-and-outward and isolating the pelvis on the syncopated Reparto snare/clave.
Shift weight laterally on 5-6-7 with a grounded knee bounce, keeping the upper torso relaxed and arms framed low in front of the waist.

followerSteps.text: Adopt a grounded, knees-bent stance and step/swivel on 1-2-3, coordinating heel-toe pivots with sharp hip/pelvic isolations.
Continue the syncopated Reparto bounce on 5-6-7, adding shoulder drops or Despelote ribcage accents on the bass hits.

commonMistakes: Standing upright with straight legs; Reparto requires a low center of gravity in the quads and ankles.
Tensing the shoulders and neck instead of keeping the upper body loose.
variations: Transitioning from Casino partnerwork into solo Reparto footwork whenever a Timba song drops into a reggaetón/reparto gear.
notes: Essential for the 'Despelote / Reparto' gear in our interactive Timba Song Player!

name: Reparto: El Taco, El Molote & El Patín (Three Havana Street Steps)
spanishName: Pasos de Reparto (El Taco, El Molote / Batidora, El Patín)
summary: Three staple Havana street Reparto steps commonly taught in Cuban dance classes: 'El Taco' (heel-drop swivel), 'El Molote / La Batidora' (rapid knee-and-hip mixer), and 'El Patín' (low sliding cross-glide).

leaderSteps.text: Counts 1-4 (El Taco): pivot on the ball of the foot while dropping/tapping the heel outward on the beat. Counts 5-8 (El Molote / Batidora): widen stance and execute rapid inward/outward knee-and-hip swivels.
Counts 9-16 (El Patín / Paso de Chocolate): glide and cross-step laterally on the balls of the feet with a low torso lean and syncopated arm checks.

followerSteps.text: Counts 1-4 (El Taco): execute sharp heel-drop pivots with hip locks. Counts 5-8 (El Molote / Batidora): sink low and drive fast knee-and-pelvic rotations from the ankles.
Counts 9-16 (El Patín): slide and cross-step smoothly across the floor while hitting the syncopated snare accents with the ribcage.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Twisting the knees without letting the heels pivot off the floor; always stay on the balls of the feet during fast knee swivels.
Holding your breath during the fast footwork.
variations: Mixing in 'El Kanguro' (low rhythmic bound) or 'La Moto' (handlebar revving gesture).
notes: UNSURE: Street Reparto step names evolve constantly across Havana barrios and teachers (e.g. El Taco, El Choco, La Batidora, El Molote, La Moto). Teachers at BOH Studios should rename or customize these three sub-steps to match their exact class callouts.

name: Rotonda > Tráfico
summary: The 'Roundabout & Traffic': an intermediate Rueda sequence where couples first orbit in a continuous roundabout ('Rotonda') and then weave past each other in two-way circle traffic ('Tráfico') before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: On 'Rotonda', lead a continuous 360-degree roundabout orbit with your partner on 1-3 and 5-7.
On 'Tráfico', release into the two-way circular weaving track on 1-3 and 5-7, passing oncoming dancers cleanly.
Continue the Tráfico weave through 1-3 and 5-7 while spotting your exit partner.
Collect the follower on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Orbit smoothly with the leader in the 'Rotonda' roundabout on 1-3 and 5-7.
Travel along the 'Tráfico' perimeter lane on 1-3 and 5-7, maintaining steady pacing.
Complete the weaving lane on 1-3 and 5-7.
Connect with the incoming leader on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Drifting out of your lane during 'Tráfico' and causing a literal traffic collision in the Rueda.
Making the 'Rotonda' orbit too wide.
variations: Calling Rotonda on its own (2 eight-counts).
notes: UNSURE: Confirm the exact lane rules for 'Rotonda' and 'Tráfico' taught at BOH Studios.

name: Rumba Arms & The Pañuelo (Handkerchief)
spanishName: Brazos de rumba y el pañuelo
summary: The upper-body framing, decoy passes, and skirt/handkerchief ('pañuelo') work that give Rumba Guaguancó and Yambú their storytelling, elegance, and visual deception.

leaderSteps.text: Hold the pañuelo (or frame open hands) with soft elbows on 1-3 and 5-7, sweeping the cloth high across the follower's line of sight as a visual decoy ('engaño') or framing her shoulders from behind.
Switch the pañuelo from hand to hand or drape it around your neck/wrists on 1-3, using a high right-hand distraction to set up a low left-hand vacunao on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Hold the edges of your skirt (or imaginary skirt/pañuelo) at hip-to-ribcage level on 1-3 and 5-7, fanning it open on the basic and sweeping it in figure-8 arcs across the front of the body.
Coordinate a high free-arm flourish with a low skirt sweep on 1-3, snapping both hands down to protect the pelvis on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Whipping the handkerchief too close to the partner's eyes or face.
Flapping the elbows up and down like wings instead of initiating the arm sweeps from the shoulder blades and ribcage.
variations: Practicing with a real handkerchief or towel in class to feel how the fabric extends your frame.
notes: Even when dancing social Timba without a prop, Cuban dancers use these exact pañuelo and skirt arm trajectories during Rumba sections.

name: Saborea
summary: 'Savor It!': a musical Rueda call where couples pause turn patterns to savor the groove with circular hip rolls, thoracic ribcage isolation, and Cuban flavour before resolving (or switching partners) into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From Enchufla or closed hold on 1-2-3, settle into a grounded stance facing your follower.
'Saborea' (savor the music) on 5-6-7 with a smooth circular cintura/ribcage roll and shoulder groove while shifting toward the next follower (or staying with your partner).
Connect in semi-closed frame on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Complete the 1-2-3 entry and soften your knees.
Savor the musical break on 5-6-7 with expressive Cuban hip figure-8 motion, ribcage isolation, and free-arm styling.
Step back on 9-11 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Rushing through the body movement with stiff knees.
Losing the count 9 pickup for Dile Que No.
variations: Saborea con Dame.
notes: Confirm whether BOH Studios switches partners on 'Saborea' or keeps the same partner.

name: Saca la Vecina
summary: 'Bring Out the Neighbour': while keeping connection with (or framing) his current partner, the leader reaches to the follower on his left/right ('la vecina') to lead an Exhíbela turn or partner switch.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea or closed hold, step 1-2-3 while reaching with your free hand to connect with the neighboring follower ('la vecina').
Lead 'la vecina' through an Exhíbela (Sácala) clockwise turn on 5-6-7 while releasing your original partner.
Collect 'la vecina' as your new partner on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Step 1-2-3 in your basic while staying aware of the neighboring leader reaching to invite you as 'la vecina'.
Step forward and execute a clean Exhíbela turn under the neighboring leader's arm on 5-6-7.
Settle into frame with that new leader on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Reaching across too far and pulling the neighbouring follower off balance while she is still connected to her previous leader.
Confusing whether 'la vecina' is the follower to the left (arriba) or right (abajo).
variations: Returning to your original partner after turning 'la vecina'.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios defines 'la vecina' as the clockwise (left) or anticlockwise (right) neighbour, and whether it changes partner permanently.

name: Saca la Vecina Doble
summary: A Rueda call where each leader turns horizontally to the neighbouring follower on his left ('la vecina'), leads her through two consecutive Exhíbela (Sacala) right turns, and then returns to his own partner (or changes partner as called).

leaderSteps.text: From Guapea or open hold, release your own partner on 1-2-3 to connect with the follower on your left ('la vecina'), and lead her into a first Exhíbela right turn on 5-6-7.
Step back-side-together on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) to check the neighbour, then lead her into a second Exhíbela right turn on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, either keep the neighbour or pivot back to your original partner on 1-2-3 and finish with a clean Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: On 1-2-3, connect with the neighbouring leader to your right and step through a first Exhíbela right turn under his raised arm on 5-6-7.
Step back-side-together in the check on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and execute a second Exhíbela right turn on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, reconnect on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Turning to the wrong side—'la vecina' is the neighbouring follower (typically to the leader's left / behind in the Rueda line of dance).
Pulling the neighbour off her spot during the two Exhíbelas so the circle spacing collapses.
Confusion on count 17 over whether the leader stays with the neighbour ('partner-change') or returns to his original partner.
variations: Finishing with 'y quédate con ella' to stay with the neighbour as a permanent backward partner change.
notes: UNSURE: Schools differ on whether 'Saca la vecina' keeps the neighbour at the end (partner change to the left) or returns to the original partner on the final Dile Que No. Confirm your school's default exit.

name: Sácala Abajo
summary: A low-framed variation of Exhíbela (Sácala) where the leader guides the follower out and around in a clockwise turn using a waist-level lead rather than an overhead arch.

leaderSteps.text: From closed hold or Guapea, step back/open on 1-2-3 while guiding the follower forward with a clear, waist-height right-hand or left-hand frame.
Lead a low-framed clockwise turn for the follower on 5-6-7 by keeping the connected hand at waist/ribcage level or lightly redirecting at the hip/back, returning to closed or Guapea frame on 7.

followerSteps.text: Step forward on 1-2 to open out as in Exhíbela, pivoting on 3 to face the leader with an engaged core.
Execute a compact clockwise turn on 5-6-7 without an overhead arm arch, keeping your elbows tucked gracefully near your ribcage.

commonMistakes: Pushing the follower's hip forcefully on count 5 instead of leading through torso rotation and a clear frame check.
Raising the hand overhead out of habit as in standard Exhíbela.
Letting the follower drift too far away on count 3.
variations: Chaining two consecutive Sácala Abajo turns before Dile Que No.
notes: UNSURE: In some Rueda schools, 'Sácala Abajo' also includes a low duck or knee bend on count 3 or 7. Verify with Enrique which styling is taught at BOH Studios.

name: Sale Tú
summary: 'You Step Out / Exit!': an advanced Rueda call where the leader (or a designated couple) steps out/ducks through the arch while the partner turns, trading places along the circle into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate an Enchufla or two-hand turn on 1-2-3.
Execute the 'Sale tú' exit pass—ducking/stepping cleanly out to the perimeter or next station on 5-6-7 while guiding the follower's turn.
Collect the next follower on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn cleanly through the 1-2-3 entry.
Complete the counter-turn on 5-6-7 as the leader exits to the next station.
Connect with the incoming leader on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Ducking with a bent neck instead of lowering with the knees.
Losing orientation in the circle on count 7.
variations: Sale Tú as a solo spotlight call in the center of the Rueda.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios uses 'Sale tú' as a specific turn-exit call or a spotlight center solo call.

name: Saloneo
summary: An elegant, Danzón- and Son-inspired conversational pause or slow promenade where the couple shows off posture, subtle hip sway, and partner connection during low-energy musical bridges.

leaderSteps.text: In closed or semi-open frame, take small, understated side-or-curving steps on 1-2-3, emphasizing upright Havana salon posture and ribcage connection.
Sway or pivot gently with the follower on 5-6-7, matching the phrasing of the piano or horn melody before re-entering Guapea.

followerSteps.text: Mirror the leader's compact salon steps on 1-2-3, keeping your weight poised over the balls of your feet and your left hand light on the leader's shoulder.
Follow the gentle torso rotation on 5-6-7 with soft figure-8 hip motion and poised head carriage.

commonMistakes: Forcing big, athletic Timba turns during a delicate salon/charanga musical passage.
Slouching the shoulders or looking down.
Losing the underlying clave pulse during the slow promenade.
variations: Adding a classic Danzón pause where the follower fans themselves on counts 5-7.
notes: Derived from the traditional Cuban Danzón 'paseo/saloneo' where couples walked and socialized during instrumental flute/violin sections.

name: Salsita
summary: A fast, syncopated Rueda combination combining an Enchufla/Setenta entry with rapid shine footwork, shoulder shimmies, and a partner change into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a crisp Enchufla or Setenta entry on 1-3 and transition into open facing position on 5-7.
Execute the 'Salsita' syncopated footwork shine and shoulder shimmy on 1-3 and 5-7 while moving toward the next follower.
Collect the new follower on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn cleanly through the 1-3 entry and face the center on 5-7.
Dance the 'Salsita' syncopated footwork and Cuban hip/shoulder styling on 1-3 and 5-7.
Connect with the incoming leader on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: Rushing the syncopated footwork and losing count 1 of the third bar.
Looking at the floor during the shine.
variations: 2-bar compact Salsita.
notes: UNSURE: Many schools have a custom choreographed shine for 'Salsita'; teacher should confirm BOH Studios' exact counts.

name: Saluda
summary: 'Greet / Salute!': after an Enchufla on 1-3, dancers pause on counts 5-7 to salute, high-five, or bow to the next partner (or across the circle) before completing the partner switch into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a clean Enchufla on 1-2-3 and release connection.
Step toward the next follower on 5-6-7 and perform a crisp salute, handshake, or high-five greeting on count 7.
Connect in semi-closed frame with the new follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Hold your perimeter station on 5-6-7 and return the incoming leader's salute or high-five on count 7.
Step back on 9-11 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Slapping the high-five too hard.
Forgetting to transition smoothly from the salute on 7 into the count 9 Dile Que No prep.
variations: Saluda a lo Cubano (chest tap and fist bump).
notes: Simple, high-spirit social icebreaker call for Improver Rueda circles.

name: Saluda a lo Moderno
summary: A playful Rueda call where leaders perform an Enchufla, greet the neighbouring follower (or the center) with a modern urban handshake/chest-bump or stylized gesture, and change partners into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3, then turn toward the neighbouring follower (or new partner) on 5-6-7 to execute the stylized 'modern greeting' (e.g. dap/fist-bump/shoulder brush).
Complete the greeting transition on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), connect in closed hold with the new partner, and lead Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the Enchufla on 1-2-3, then turn on 5-6-7 to perform the synchronized modern greeting with the incoming or neighbouring leader.
Finish the gesture on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), connect in frame on count 12, and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Getting carried away with the greeting gesture and missing the count 13 Dile Que No.
Stopping the basic footwork pulse while performing the hand/body greeting.
Turning to the wrong side of the circle for the greeting.
variations: Greeting the neighbour on the left first on 5-7, then greeting the new partner on the right on 9-11.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm the exact greeting gesture (fist bump, hip bump, or two-part neighbour greeting) used in the Bournemouth classes.

name: Se Viró
summary: A Rueda orientation-flip call ('it turned inside out!') that reverses the circle from standard inward-facing Rueda to outward-facing Rueda (Pa'Fuera), or vice versa, without changing partners.

leaderSteps.text: From standard Guapea, step 1-2-3 while pivoting 180 degrees with the partner (or leading an inside turn pivot) so that your back now faces the center of the Rueda circle. Pause on 4.
Execute a Dile Que No on 5-6-7 along the new outward-facing orientation (Rueda Pa'Fuera), establishing Guapea facing the outside of the room. Pause on 8.

followerSteps.text: Follow the leader's frame rotation on 1-2-3 to pivot 180 degrees so that you are oriented for outward-facing Rueda. Pause on 4.
Travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 along the inverted circle geometry, finishing on 7 facing the leader with the center of the circle behind him. Pause on 8.

commonMistakes: Trying to turn back toward the center of the circle during the Dile Que No on 5-6-7 out of habit.
Confusing which direction 'Dame' goes once the Rueda is flipped inside-out.
Backing too far into the center of the circle and colliding with other leaders' backs.
variations: Calling 'Se viró' a second time to flip the Rueda from Pa'Fuera back to normal.
notes: UNSURE: In some Rueda systems 'Se viró' flips the circle to Rueda Pa'Fuera (backs to center), while in others it is a sudden mid-step 180-degree direction reversal during a walking call (like 'Paséala > se viró'). Confirm which usage applies here.

name: Seis y Nueve
summary: An interlocking circular Casino/Rueda figure where leader and follower wrap into opposing side-by-side or hammerlock arcs (forming the shapes of a 6 and a 9 from above) and rotate together before unwrapping into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: From a two-hand hold, lead the follower into a right hammerlock on 1-3, then turn inward under the joined arm on 5-7 so you are standing hip-to-hip facing opposite directions (the 6 and the 9).
Walk forward in a tight shared circle on 1-3, then raise the arms sequentially on 5-7 to unwrap both hammerlocks.
Open the frame on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right into the hammerlock on 1-3 and take compact steps on 5-7 as the leader wraps alongside you facing the opposite way.
Rotate together around your shared axis on 1-3 and pivot cleanly out of the unwrap on 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling apart while both dancers are wrapped in opposite-facing hammerlocks; stay close hip-to-hip with bent elbows.
Clamping thumbs during the unwrap.
variations: Seis y Nueve con Dame (changing partners on the exit).
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios teaches 'Seis y Nueve' as an opposite-facing double hammerlock or a 2-bar Enchufla partner switch.

name: Setenta por las Manos
summary: A sleek, technical variation of Setenta where the leader guides all transitions purely through low wrist/hand rolls, waist-level switches, and micro-led frame checks without large overhead swings.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate Setenta on 1-3, then use a compact hand-to-hand roll and low waist-level switch on 5-7 to exchange places.
Lead a continuous series of inside and outside turns on 1-3 and 5-7 using subtle finger-hook tension and behind-the-back hand transfers.
Collect the follower in open frame on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Setenta entry on 1-3 and keep your hands poised near waist/ribcage height on 5-7 to feel the subtle hand-to-hand transfers.
Maintain an engaged core and light hook tension through the turns on 1-3 and 5-7, never letting your arms go limp or overly rigid.
Step back on 1-3 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Twisting the partner's wrist instead of rolling the palms around each other.
Chasing the follower's hands instead of placing your hand at a predictable waist-level target zone.
Losing the circular Casino geometry while focusing on hand tricks.
variations: Combining with mid-figure rhythm reversals on counts 9-16.
notes: UNSURE: 'Setenta por las manos' (or 'por abajo') varies by teacher; confirm with Enrique which exact hand-switch sequence is canonical at BOH Studios.

name: Setenta y Cinco (75)
summary: A classic numbered member of the Setenta family that follows the initial hammerlock entry with an alternating sequence of overhead loops and a directional turn check before Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Enter with a two-hand hold into the standard Setenta hammerlock on 1-3, then exchange places around the circle on 5-7 while retaining both hands.
On 1-3, raise the left hand to unwrap or redirect the follower while keeping the right hand connected, then on 5-7 bring the right hand over your own head to step through into a shared cross wrap.
Unwind the follower's final turn on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right under the leader's raised left arm into the Setenta hammerlock on 1-3, and travel smoothly around the circle on 5-7 with your right hand resting softly at your waist.
Follow the overhead lead on 1-3 to pivot cleanly, and maintain small circular steps on 5-7 while the leader turns under the right arm.
Complete the exit turn on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Lifting the hammerlocked back hand toward the follower's shoulder blades instead of keeping it low at the hip.
Gripping with thumbs during the two-hand overhead switches.
Taking wide steps that pull the arms taut on counts 9-16.
variations: Finishing with a Siete hook turn before Dile Que No.
notes: UNSURE: Numbered Setenta variations (71, 72, 75) have slight regional differences in whether the leader or follower turns on 9-11 vs 13-15. Teacher should verify BOH Studios' exact count breakdown.

name: Setenta y Dos (72)
summary: An advanced numbered variation of Setenta (70) incorporating a double hammerlock switch, an behind-the-back or overhead leader turn, and a continuous two-hand unwrap.

leaderSteps.text: Execute the Setenta entry into the follower's hammerlock on 1-3 and exchange places on 5-7 while keeping both hands connected.
Lead an inside/outside direction reversal on 1-3 while turning into your own hammerlock or overhead pass on 5-7.
Unwind both arms cleanly on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right into the Setenta hammerlock on 1-3 and walk across on 5-7 with a relaxed right elbow.
