Follow the leader's check and turn reversal on 1-3, stepping compactly around the circle on 5-7.
Unwind on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Jerking the hammerlocked arm during the count 9-11 reversal.
Stepping too wide and losing the compact circular orbit.
Clamping thumbs.
variations: Chaining Setenta y Uno (71) directly into Setenta y Dos (72).
notes: UNSURE: Verify exact count-by-count hand switches for 72 with Enrique, as schools differ on 72 vs 75.

name: Setenta y Uno (71)
summary: An extension of Setenta (70) where, after the initial hammerlock entry and Enchufla-style exchange, the leader retains the two-hand hold for an extra wrap or hook turn before resolving with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Execute the standard Setenta entry on 1-3 into the follower's hammerlock, and lead the Enchufla-style place exchange on 5-7 while keeping both hands connected.
Raise the right hand over the follower's head on 1-3 to unwrap the hammerlock, then on 5-7 drape or hook-turn into a secondary wrap without releasing the grip.
Unwind the final turn on 1-3 and lead Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right into the Setenta hammerlock on 1-3 and exchange places with the leader on 5-7 while keeping your right elbow soft.
Turn under the raised right hand on 1-3 and follow the continuous circular lead on 5-7.
Complete the exit turn on 1-3 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Twisting the follower's wrist during the continuous two-hand transitions; use a loose two-finger hook grip so the hands can rotate freely.
Dropping the left hand out of habit on count 5 as in basic Setenta.
Losing the circular trajectory.
variations: Setenta y Uno con Alarde (adding a free-hand styling check).
notes: Safety reminder: both dancers must keep a rotating hook grip (no thumbs clamped) whenever both hands stay connected past count 8.

name: Sho'boun' (German Mesa)
summary: A stylized Rueda call combining an Enchufla entry with a rhythmic tabletop/bouncing groove ('German mesa' variation) in the center before advancing to the next partner with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla on 1-2-3 to swap places and face the center of the circle, then drop into the signature rhythmic knee-bend/tabletop ('mesa') groove with arm styling on 5-6-7.
Complete the second half of the rhythmic groove on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) while travelling counter-clockwise to the next follower, and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Turn left in the opening Enchufla on 1-2-3, then mirror the rhythmic 'mesa' groove and body bounce along the outer ring on 5-6-7.
Finish the groove on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), connect with the arriving leader on count 12, and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Bending forward from the lower back with a rounded spine during the 'mesa' groove instead of hinging at the hips and knees with a supported core.
Losing the count 12 connection for the final Dile Que No.
Forgetting whether the call advances one partner or returns to the same partner.
variations: Adding a vocal chant on counts 5-7 and 9-11.
notes: UNSURE: The name 'Sho'boun' (German mesa)' is unusual and specific to a local or festival routine. Teachers should confirm the exact spelling, vocal call, arm choreography, and whether it changes partners.

name: Síguelo
summary: A continuation modifier call in Rueda ('keep it going!') that instructs dancers to stay in the current groove, mambo step, or repeating pattern instead of exiting into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Instead of initiating the usual exit or Dile Que No, maintain the active footwork or body movement pattern from the preceding call (e.g. mambo steps, rumba guaguancó, or continuous Enchuflas) on 1-2-3. Pause on 4.
Continue the repeating pattern on 5-6-7 while listening for the caller's next exit cue (such as 'Dile Que No' or 'Dame'). Pause on 8.

followerSteps.text: Keep executing the current groove or repeating figure on 1-2-3 rather than prepping for a Dile Que No exit. Pause on 4.
Continue matching the pattern on 5-6-7 while maintaining visual and frame awareness for when the caller ends the loop. Pause on 8.

commonMistakes: Exiting automatically into Dile Que No on count 5 because the dancer memorized a fixed length for the previous move instead of listening to the caller.
Letting the energy or step precision drop during the extended repetition.
Leaders giving mixed frame signals when transitioning from 'Síguelo' back into the exit call.
variations: Enchufla con mambo > Síguelo (holding the center mambo shine across multiple eight-counts).
Dame > Síguelo (continuing to change partners on every eight-count).
notes: Does not change partners on its own unless attached to a partner-changing loop (like 'Dame > síguelo'). Teach students to treat 'Síguelo' as an infinite loop until the caller gives a termination call.

name: Sombrero Complicado
summary: An extended multi-turn combination that chains a classic Sombrero entry with a Setenta hammerlock, an overhead neck-drape switch, and a final Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Enter with a two-hand crossed hold on 1-3, turning the follower right, and drape the right hand over your own head on 5-7 while keeping the left hand low in a hammerlock.
Exchange places on 1-3, then raise both hands in sequence on 5-7 to complete the classic Sombrero drape over the follower's shoulders.
Open into closed/semi-closed frame on 1-3 and lead Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right on 1-3 into the two-hand wrap and walk around the circle on 5-7 while keeping your lower-back hand relaxed.
Follow the continuous two-hand lead on 1-3 and pivot into the Sombrero shoulder drape on 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 and travel cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling on the hammerlock hand while executing the overhead Sombrero drape; keep the lower hand soft at waist level.
Losing the circular slot and drifting sideways across the floor.
Forgetting to release thumbs during the two-hand turns.
variations: Finishing with a Mambo check on counts 17-20 before Dile Que No.
notes: A staple intermediate social floor combination; teachers should check whether the BOH Studios version is 2 or 3 eight-counts.

name: Sombrero con Mambo
summary: A musical variation of Sombrero where, once the two-hand hat wrap settles over the follower's shoulders on count 7, the couple dances a synchronized Mambo groove in the wrap before Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Take a two-hand crossed hold (right over left), turn the follower right on 1-3, and drape both arms over both heads on 5-7 into the classic Sombrero wrap.
Keep the Sombrero shoulder wrap connected and dance a rhythmic Mambo forward-and-back basic with the follower on 1-3 and 5-7.
Open into semi-closed frame on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right on 1-3 under the crossed hands and settle into the Sombrero shoulder wrap on 5-7.
Match the leader's Mambo steps and Cuban hip/ribcage groove on 1-3 and 5-7 while wrapped in the Sombrero frame.
Step back on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Pulling down on the follower's shoulders during the Mambo section; let the forearms rest weightlessly.
Rushing straight into Dile Que No on count 9 and forgetting the Mambo section.
variations: Sombrero con Mambo y Dame (changing partners on the final Dile Que No).
notes: No partner change unless followed by 'Dame'. Great for teaching students not to rush out of wraps.

name: Sombrero Nuevo
summary: A modern twist on the classic Sombrero where the two-hand entry includes an extra leader turn or reversed hand-cross so the 'hat' drapes over both dancers or transitions into a double wrap.

leaderSteps.text: Take a two-hand crossed hold and lead the follower's right turn on 1-3 while simultaneously pivoting or switching the top hand of the cross.
Drape both arms smoothly over the head(s) in the Sombrero hat action on 5-6-7.
Lead a secondary unwrap turn on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn right on the spot on 1-3 with elbows bent in front of your ribcage and a loose two-finger hook.
Step 5-6-7 as the Sombrero loop settles over the shoulders, keeping posture tall.
Unwind smoothly on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Yanking both hands down over the partner's head on count 5; let the elbows float wide to clear the head and glasses/earrings.
Crossing the wrong hand on top at count 1, resulting in a locked wrist.
Standing too far apart during the Sombrero drape.
variations: Sombrero Doble (draping over the leader's head on 3 and the follower's head on 5).
notes: UNSURE: Verify whether BOH Studios defines 'Sombrero Nuevo' as Sombrero Doble (both heads) or Sombrero with an inside leader turn on 1-3.

name: Sombrero y Plancha
summary: A classic Sombrero variation where, after draping the two-hand hat wrap over the shoulders, the couple executes a smooth 'plancha' (ironing/sliding arm or torso wave check) before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Take a crossed two-hand hold (right over left), turn the follower right on 1-3, and drape both arms over both heads into the Sombrero wrap on 5-7.
Execute the 'Plancha' action on 1-3 and 5-7 (gliding/ironing the connected hands smoothly across or leading a supported core torso check) without dropping the partner's weight.
Open into semi-closed frame on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn right on 1-3 and settle into the Sombrero shoulder wrap on 5-7.
Follow the 'Plancha' arm glide or torso wave on 1-3 and 5-7 while keeping 100% of your weight over your own feet.
Step back on 1-3 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Never turn 'Plancha' into an unled floor drop or heavy back dip in a moving Rueda circle; both dancers must stay self-supported on their own legs.
Pulling down on the follower's neck during the Sombrero drape.
variations: Sombrero y Plancha con Dame.
notes: UNSURE: In some Cuban schools 'plancha' is a horizontal ironing hand-slide across the chest/stomach after Sombrero, while in others it is a torso lean check. Verify with Enrique.

name: Son Montuno (Closed-Position Basic & Turns)
summary: The bridge between classic Son Cubano and modern Casino: danced in an intimate, upright closed frame on contratiempo timing (2-3-4, 6-7-8) with compact rotating basics and unhurried underarm turns.

leaderSteps.text: In closed hold, pause/settle hip on 1, step left foot side/forward on 2, and shift weight on 3-4; pause on 5, step right foot side/back on 6, and shift weight on 7-8 while rotating slowly around your shared axis.
Lead a smooth, unhurried clockwise turn for the follower on 2-3-4 under your raised left arm, and draw her gently back into closed embrace on 6-7-8.

followerSteps.text: In closed hold, pause/settle hip on 1, step right foot side/back on 2, and shift weight on 3-4; pause on 5, step left foot side/forward on 6, and shift weight on 7-8 with poised posture.
Execute a calm, compact turn on 2-3-4 keeping steps directly underneath your hips, and settle smoothly back into closed embrace on 6-7-8.

commonMistakes: Rushing back onto count 1 when the bass tumbao and congas are pulling you onto 2-3-4.
Leading aggressive, fast Timba turns instead of keeping Son Montuno intimate, musical, and compact.
variations: Adding a Tornillo (slow leader pivot) or Paseo walk in Son timing.
notes: When a modern Timba track opens with a traditional piano/tres intro (like Havana D'Primera or Pupy), starting in Son Montuno before switching to A Tiempo Casino on the montuno drop is top-tier musicality.

name: Suzie Q
summary: A classic jazz-and-mambo crossover shine adapted with grounded Cuban knee bounce and ribcage groove, crossing one foot in front while pivoting on the heel/ball of the foot.

leaderSteps.text: Cross left foot in front of right on 1 (swiveling on the heel/ball), step right foot small to the right side on 2, and cross left foot in front again on 3.
Switch sides on 4/5: cross right foot in front of left on 5, step left foot small to the left side on 6, and cross right foot in front on 7.

followerSteps.text: Cross right foot in front of left on 1 (or left in solo line-up), step small to the side on 2, and cross in front again on 3 with Cuban hip and shoulder groove.
Reverse direction on 5-6-7, crossing the opposite foot in front on 5, stepping side on 6, and crossing on 7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Twisting the knee joint while the foot is planted flat; let the heel/ball pivot freely with the hip.
Dancing Suzie Q upright and stiff instead of sinking into a grounded Cuban Songo/Timba bounce.
variations: Cuban Suzie Q with double shoulder/ribcage hits on 1 and 3.
notes: In Cuban Suelta, Suzie Q is danced lower into the knees with more ribcage isolation than the upright ballroom/NY mambo version.

name: Tacón-Punta
summary: Solo Cuban timba footwork alternating crisp heel digs and toe taps to accent brass hits and syncopated rhythms during suelta or mambo sections.

leaderSteps.text: Strike the left heel forward on 1 (toe flexed upward), tap the left toe back or beside the standing right foot on 2, and step onto the left foot in place on 3 with grounded knee flexion. Pause on 4.
Strike the right heel forward on 5, tap the right toe beside the left foot on 6, and transfer full weight onto the right foot on 7. Pause on 8.

followerSteps.text: Mirror or perform the same solo footwork: dig the right (or left, if dancing in unison) heel forward on 1, tap the toe back on 2, and step onto the working foot in place on 3. Pause on 4.
Dig the opposite heel forward on 5, tap the toe in on 6, and step firmly onto that foot on 7 while allowing natural Cuban hip and ribcage movement. Pause on 8.

commonMistakes: Locking the standing knee during the heel strike, which makes the upper body stiff and bounces the head.
Placing full body weight onto the heel or toe taps on counts 1-2 or 5-6 instead of keeping weight over the standing leg until count 3 and 7.
Looking down at the feet instead of maintaining posture and visual connection with the partner or group.
variations: Double-time syncopated taps (1-and-2-and-3) during high-energy mambo brass riffs.
Angling the torso 45 degrees left and right to match the working foot.
Adding a slight hop or chassé transition on count 4 and 8.
notes: UNSURE: Teachers vary on whether Tacón-Punta starts on the left or right foot in suelta lines, and whether it is taught as heel-toe-step (1-2-3) or double heel-toe across 1-2-3-4. Confirm preferred school footwork phrasing.

name: Tijeras
summary: The 'Scissors': an athletic figure where the leader's and follower's arms or circular paths cross and uncross in a scissor-like action with alternating turns.

leaderSteps.text: From a two-hand hold, lead an initial cross-wrap on 1-3 where the arms scissor across the center line.
Step around the circle on 5-6-7 while uncrossing/re-crossing the arms overhead as both partners pivot.
Release the scissor wrap cleanly on 9-11 and finish with Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Turn into the crossed-arm scissor position on 1-3, keeping your elbows tucked in front of your ribs.
Pivot smoothly on 5-6-7 as the arms uncross overhead, maintaining your own vertical axis.
Step back on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Scissoring the arms forcefully at face or neck height; keep overhead passes high and waist-level passes low.
Locking the wrists during the cross.
Over-stepping on counts 5-7.
variations: Tijeras Complicado (adding an extra hammerlock switch).
notes: UNSURE: 'Tijeras' refers to a specific two-hand scissor wrap in some schools and a split/scissor footwork check in others. Teacher should verify which version is taught at BOH Studios.

name: Tijeras Complicado
summary: An extended, high-velocity version of Tijeras ('Scissors') that adds an extra hammerlock wrap, a leader duck-under, and a syncopated unwind before Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Enter with the Tijeras crossed-arm scissor wrap on 1-3 and execute the first overhead uncross/re-cross on 5-7.
Instead of exiting, duck under the top arm on 1-3 to create a reverse scissor lock, then turn the follower through the window on 5-7.
Unwind the final scissor wrap on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn into the initial Tijeras cross on 1-3 and pivot smoothly through the first overhead pass on 5-7.
Keep your frame compact on 1-3 as the leader ducks under, then turn cleanly through the window on 5-7.
Unwind on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Forcing the scissor arm switches at high speed without letting the wrists rotate in a loose hook grip.
SAFETY: Ducking with a rounded back instead of bending the knees.
Pulling the follower off her vertical axis.
variations: Finishing with an Enchufla Doble into a Rueda partner change.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm the exact 2nd eight-count variation of Tijeras Complicado taught at BOH Studios.

name: Tobillo
summary: A playful Rueda partner-change call where an Enchufla on 1-3 is followed by a light, controlled ankle-to-ankle tap on counts 5-7 before advancing to the next follower for Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Enchufla on 1-2-3, trading places with your current follower.
Step toward the inside of the circle on 5-6 and gently brush or tap the inside of your ankle against your partner's (or incoming partner's) ankle on count 7 while keeping your standing knee soft.
Step to the next follower on your right on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Step in place on the outer perimeter on 5-6 and lightly tap the inside of your ankle against the leader's ankle on count 7 without losing your vertical axis.
Connect with the incoming leader on 9-11 and travel smoothly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Kicking or swinging the foot forcefully into the partner's anklebone; the contact must be a gentle, controlled brush.
Leaning the upper body sideways and losing balance while lifting the foot on count 7.
variations: Tobillo Doble (tapping right ankle then left ankle before switching partners).
notes: Hand signal: caller points down toward the ankle or lifts a foot slightly to tap the ankle. UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios taps the ankle of the outgoing partner on 7 or the incoming partner.

name: Toma Eléctrica
summary: The 'Electric Socket / Shock': an explosive, high-energy advanced Timba figure featuring a rapid wrap, a sudden musical freeze or 'electric shock' body-vibration accent (Tembleque), and a whip-fast unwind.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a fast two-hand wrap or Siete Loco entry on 1-3, locking into a side-by-side or sweetheart presentation wrap on 5-7.

On count 1 (or the musical bloque), trigger the 'Toma Eléctrica'—a sudden freeze and high-frequency Tembleque body vibration with the follower through 1-3, then launch into a rapid unwind turn on 5-7.
Complete the final directional check on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Spin into the two-hand wrap on 1-3 and settle into the connected frame on 5-7 with grounded knees.
React instantly to the leader's frame check on 1 with an 'electric shock' Tembleque shake on 1-3, then spot sharply through the fast unwind on 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Shaking the follower's shoulders or neck violently during the 'electric shock' accent; the Tembleque vibration must be generated internally by each dancer's own knees/core, never by shaking your partner!
SAFETY: Yanking the fast unwind turn on count 5 after the freeze.
Missing the musical break/bloque that makes the figure hit.
variations: In Rueda de Casino, all couples freeze and vibrate simultaneously on the caller's shout before switching partners.
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether BOH Studios teaches Toma Eléctrica as a partner wrap with Tembleque or a specific Rueda partner-switch call.

name: Toma Eléctrica Complicado
summary: An advanced Rueda figure building on Toma Eléctrica with two-hand wraps, duck-unders, a high-frequency body-vibration/shock accent ('eléctrica'), and a partner change into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Connect both hands on 1-2-3 to lead a Setenta/Sombrero-style entry, wrapping the follower on 5-6-7.
Duck under the raised arm bridge on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) into a close side-by-side or shadow check, and trigger the 'eléctrica' tembleque/shock accent on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, unwind the follower with an Enchufla-style hand switch on 1-2-3 and send her into an outside turn on 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, release to advance to the next follower on 1-2-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Take the two-hand connection on 1-2-3 and turn into the wrap on 5-6-7 while keeping elbows relaxed and in front of the ribcage.
Maintain the overhead arch as the leader ducks under on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), then hit the 'eléctrica' body vibration/tembleque accent with him on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, follow the unwrapping turn on 1-2-3 and complete the free or guided turn on 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, receive the incoming leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: During the wrap and duck-under, keep a light hook grip without thumbs and never yank the follower's arm during the 'eléctrica' vibration.
Hitting the 'eléctrica' shock accent through the arms instead of isolating it in the ribcage and shoulders.
Rushing the unwrapping turns on counts 17-24.
variations: Keeping the same partner on counts 25-32 if called without Dame.
notes: UNSURE: 'Toma Eléctrica Complicado' is a signature routine call whose exact hand switches and count length vary by school. Teacher should verify the exact 8-count breakdown.

name: Triple Play
summary: The extension of Doble Play: after the initial Enchufla, the leader chains passes/checks past two followers ('first and second base') and picks up the third follower along the circle into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla with your starting follower on 1-3, then travel to the first follower on your right on 5-7 with a check/clap.
Continue to the second follower on 1-3 (or execute a quick Enchufla pass) and advance toward the third follower on 5-7.
Collect the third follower on 1-3 and finish with Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Execute the starting Enchufla on 1-3 and hold your perimeter station on 5-7 with a rhythmic basic.
Maintain the outer circle on 1-3 and 5-7, clapping or turning as passing leaders complete the first and second bases.
Connect with the third incoming leader on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: Losing count of how many followers you have passed and stopping at the wrong station.
Cutting straight across the middle of the Rueda and causing a traffic jam.
variations: Shouting '¡Uno! ¡Dos! ¡Tres!' as the Rueda hits each base.
notes: Requires at least 4–5 couples in the Rueda circle to feel spacious.

name: Tumba Francesa
summary: A culturally rich Rueda call that weaves the stately, rhythmic court-and-drum posture of eastern Cuba's Tumba Francesa tradition (or a syncopated cross-body pass) into the circle before resolving into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate the figure on 1-2-3 with upright, regal posture and a smooth rotational lead.
Guide the follower through the stately Tumba Francesa cadence and frame check on 5-6-7.
Open into semi-closed hold on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Step 1-2-3 with poised upper-body carriage and subtle skirt/arm styling.
Follow the leader's rotational cadence on 5-6-7 with grounded footwork.
Step back on 9-11 and travel smoothly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Dancing with hunched shoulders instead of the proud, upright posture characteristic of Oriente's Tumba Francesa.
Rushing the steps.
variations: Tumba Francesa con Dame.
notes: UNSURE: In some Rueda circles 'Tumba Francesa' is a specific 2-bar turn/pass pattern rather than a folkloric styling break. Teacher should verify BOH Studios' version.

name: Tumba Francesa Complicado
summary: An intricate Rueda call combining elegant Franco-Haitian/Oriente-inspired paseo turns, multi-hand wraps, and synchronized curtsy/bow checks before changing partners in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Initiate with an elegant cross-hand or two-hand Paseo turn on 1-2-3, wrapping the follower into a side-by-side promenade check on 5-6-7.
Lead a synchronized directional pivot and stately Mason/Tumba Francesa bow check on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), then unwind the follower across the front on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, execute a leader hook turn under the raised arm on 1-2-3 followed by a follower Exhíbela on 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, release to advance to the next partner on 1-2-3 and close with a smooth Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Step through the opening turn on 1-2-3 and settle into the side-by-side wrap on 5-6-7 with tall, regal posture.
Match the directional pivot and subtle curtsy/skirt-flair accent on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), then unwind smoothly on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).
On counts 17-24, maintain frame as the leader turns on 1-2-3, then execute the Exhíbela turn on 5-6-7.
On counts 25-32, connect with the arriving leader on 1-2-3 and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Safety: Keep all wrap and behind-the-back hand changes at waist level with soft wrists so the follower's shoulder is never hyperextended.
Dancing the figure with heavy, hunched posture instead of the upright, elegant carriage referencing Tumba Francesa.
Losing the circular Rueda station during the promenade section.
variations: Finishing with the same partner if no Dame is called at the end.
notes: UNSURE: 'Tumba Francesa Complicado' choreography varies significantly between Rueda masters (some emphasize a hammerlock promenade, others a multi-couple star/wheel). Teacher must confirm the exact sequence taught in class.

name: Un Tarro
summary: The 'Bull Horn': the quickest partner-change call in Rueda de Casino—starting from closed position (or Guapea), the leader steps directly backward/anticlockwise on 1-3 to hook the next follower without a Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Release your current follower on count 1 and step backward/anticlockwise along the circle on 1-2-3 to arrive directly in front of the next follower.
Connect immediately in closed hold (or Guapea) with the new follower on 5-6-7, continuing the basic step without a Dile Que No transition.

followerSteps.text: Continue your basic step in place along the circle on 1-2-3 while keeping your frame ready as your current leader steps back.
Connect seamlessly in closed hold (or Guapea) with the new leader arriving in front of you on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Leaders stepping backward blindly on 1-2-3 without glancing over their shoulder to check spacing.
Trying to lead a Dile Que No on 5-7 when the Rueda is staying in closed 'Arriba' position.
Bumping elbows with the incoming follower.
variations: Un Tarro con Mentira (faking the step back on 1-3 and returning to the same partner on 5-7).
notes: Hand signal: caller places index and pinky fingers (or two index fingers) on the forehead like bull horns ('poner los tarros' is Cuban slang for cheating on a partner!).

name: Un Tarro sin Soltar
summary: A Rueda variation of Tarro where the leader ducks under his raised left arm as if moving to the next partner, but never lets go of his current follower's hand ('sin soltar'), bringing her back into Dile Que No without changing partners.

leaderSteps.text: Step forward on 1-2-3 raising the left arm to duck underneath in the Tarro motion toward the next partner, but maintain the left-to-right hand hold ('sin soltar') and pivot on 5-6-7 to face your original follower.
Lead your original follower into an inside turn or stabilizing check on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and finish with Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Keep a light, continuous hook connection in the right hand as the leader ducks under on 1-2-3, and turn smoothly in place on 5-6-7 without releasing him.
Complete the return turn on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) into closed hold and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Safety: Leaders travelling too far toward the next follower while still holding their original partner's hand, which yanks the original follower's shoulder—stay close when executing 'sin soltar' and keep knees bent during the duck-under.
Followers letting go of the hand on count 3 out of muscle memory from regular Tarro.
Twisting the follower's wrist during the underarm duck—use a loose finger hook so the hand swivels freely.
variations: 1-eight-count compact version (Tarro sin soltar on 1-3, immediate Dile Que No on 5-7, similar to Prima).
notes: Mechanically very close to Prima, except the leader sells the body language of a travelling Tarro before rebounding back to his partner.

name: Una Media
summary: A Rueda partner-change call where an Enchufla entry is followed by a half-circle hook or 180-degree check in the center before advancing to the next follower for Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a clean Enchufla on 1-2-3, trading places with your follower.
Step into the center lane on 5-6-7, executing the half-turn ('media') check or hooking your right arm briefly with the follower before releasing to move anticlockwise.
Collect the next follower on 9-11 and complete Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Complete the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Execute the matching half-turn check on the outer perimeter on 5-6-7 while spotting the incoming leader.
Step back on 9-11 and walk cleanly through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Over-rotating the half-turn into a full 360-degree spin and arriving late on count 9.
SAFETY: Pulling on the hooked elbow if using the arm-hook variation.
variations: Media Doble (extending the turn sequence over an extra bar).
notes: UNSURE: 'Una Media' varies between Rueda syllabi (in some a half-turn Enchufla check, in others a Sock/Ankle touch play on 'media' = sock). Teacher should verify BOH Studios' version.

name: Una Pa' Ti, Una Pa' Mí
spanishName: Una pa' ti, una pa' mí
summary: 'One for You, One for Me': an alternating Rueda call where the leader leads one turn/Pelota for the follower ('una pa' ti'), one for himself ('una pa' mí'), and switches partners into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead the follower's turn/exchange on 1-3 ('una pa' ti') and execute your own matching turn/check on 5-7 ('una pa' mí').
Complete the secondary exchange on 1-3 and advance to the next follower on 5-7.
Connect with the new follower on 1-3 and lead Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Execute your turn on 1-3 ('una pa' ti') and frame the leader's turn on 5-7 ('una pa' mí').
Follow the secondary exchange on 1-3 and hold your perimeter station on 5-7.
Step back on 1-3 with the incoming leader and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: Pulling on the connected hand during the alternating turns.
Forgetting to switch partners at the end of the sequence.
variations: 2-bar fast Una Pa' Ti, Una Pa' Mí.
notes: Closely related to 'Por mí, por ti'; verify any count differences in the BOH Studios syllabus.

name: Vacílala Completa
summary: A full-cycle Vacílala where the follower executes her traveling clockwise turn on 1-3 and continues around the circle on 5-7 (or executes a second turn) before the leader picks her up for Dile Que No on 9-15.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea, lead a clean Vacílala turn on 1-2-3.
Instead of closing on 5, guide or mirror the follower along the full circular arc on 5-6-7.
Collect the follower in semi-closed frame on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the traveling clockwise Vacílala turn on 1-2-3.
Continue traveling smoothly along the circular orbit (or complete the secondary turn) on 5-6-7 with poised posture.
Step back into the leader's frame on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Grabbing the follower prematurely on count 5 when a full 2-bar 'Vacílala Completa' was called.
Spinning in place instead of traveling around the circle.
variations: Vacílala Completa con Dame (picking up the next follower on count 9).
notes: Confirm whether BOH Studios uses 'Vacílala Completa' to distinguish a 2-bar Vacílala + Dile Que No from a 1-bar Vacílala.

name: Vacílala con Bamboleo
summary: A musical, Timba-infused variation of Vacílala where the free turn opens into a low-grounded 'bamboleo' (swaying body isolation / Despelote groove) before reconnecting for Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a clean Vacílala free turn for the follower on 1-3 while stepping around the circular arc.
Instead of immediately picking up the follower in closed hold, face the follower in open Suelta on 5-6-7 and sink into a grounded 'bamboleo' (lateral ribcage/hip sway and shoulder groove).
Continue the playful Bamboleo interaction on 9-11, then reconnect smoothly on 12 to lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the traveling clockwise Vacílala turn on 1-2-3, spotting the leader on 3.
Catch the visual cue from the leader and drop into a fluid 'bamboleo' sway (thoracic isolation and Cuban hip pendulum) on 5-6-7.
Finish the solo body-movement groove on 9-11, offer your frame on 12, and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Grabbing the follower on count 5 when she is mid-groove.
Doing the Bamboleo sway with stiff knees or losing the underlying clave timing.
Forgetting to re-establish visual and physical connection by count 12 for Dile Que No.
variations: Extending the Bamboleo groove for an extra eight-count during a Bamboleo or Havana D'Primera bomba/mambo breakdown.
notes: Named in homage to Lazarito Valdés y Bamboleo and the swaying Timba body isolation style.

name: Vacílala con Cero
summary: A Rueda combination where the leader initiates a Vacílala turn for the follower on counts 1-3, then circles completely around her ('con cero') while she finishes her turn, before changing partners or closing with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Prep on 1 and give a gentle right-to-right (or left-to-right) impulse on 2-3 to send the follower into a free Vacílala right turn, then immediately travel in a full 360-degree loop ('cero') around her on 5-6-7.
Complete the orbit on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11), advancing to the next follower (or reconnecting with the current follower), and lead Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Step 1-2-3 into a free clockwise Vacílala turn, then step forward-side-together in place along the circle on 5-6-7 while the leader orbits around you.
Mark in place on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) as the leader finishes the loop, connect into closed hold on count 12, and travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Leaders starting their circular orbit too early on count 2 and cutting across the follower's turning path.
Followers travelling too far forward during the Vacílala on 5-6-7 instead of staying on the circle perimeter so the leader has room to orbit.
Over-spinning the follower with a heavy arm push on count 3.
variations: Vacílala con cero y dame (explicitly advancing to the next partner after completing the orbit).
notes: UNSURE: Verify whether your school keeps the same partner at the end of 'Vacílala con Cero' or automatically transitions into a Dame partner change on counts 9-15.

name: Vacílala con Columbia
summary: An explosive Afro-Cuban fusion figure where the Vacílala turn breaks open into a fast, athletic Rumba Columbia footwork challenge before reconnecting into Casino.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a crisp Vacílala free turn on 1-3, opening the space between you and the follower.
Drop into an athletic Rumba Columbia stance on 5-6-7, executing fast syncopated heel-toe/cross footwork and sharp shoulder/arm accents.
Resolve the Columbia shine on 9-11, re-establish open frame connection on 12, and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Complete the traveling Vacílala turn on 1-2-3 and face the leader.
Answer the leader's Columbia challenge with sharp solo footwork, rhythmic skirt work, or Changó/Ochún-inspired arm styling on 5-6-7.
Finish the solo exchange on 9-11 and step cleanly into Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Kicking or lunging too wide in the Columbia footwork on a crowded social dance floor.
Losing the 1-2-3, 5-6-7 Casino count when switching into 6/8 or syncopated Columbia rhythms.
Abruptly yanking the follower back into partnerwork on count 13.
variations: Incorporating a subtle vacunao / defense play on count 11 before Dile Que No.
notes: Ideal for Timba tracks that feature a sudden Rumba or 6/8 percussion break mid-montuno.

name: Vacílala y Dame
summary: A classic Rueda partner-change figure where the leader leads his current follower into a free Vacílala right turn on the first eight-count, leaves her to travel to the next follower on his right, and finishes with Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Step back on 1, give a clear, light Vacílala turn impulse on 2-3 releasing the follower to turn solo, and on 5-6-7 walk counter-clockwise toward the next follower in the circle.
Connect with the new follower in closed hold on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and lead her across the slot in a Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

followerSteps.text: Execute a smooth clockwise right turn on 1-2-3 and continue stepping along the outside circumference on 5-6-7 while turning to face the center.
Step back-side-together on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) as the new leader connects from the left, then travel through Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (counts 13-15).

commonMistakes: Leaders abandoning the current follower on count 1 before actually giving her the Vacílala turn lead on 2-3.
Followers continuing to walk forward into the next couple's space on 5-6-7 instead of turning in their own station to face the incoming leader.
Rushing the Dame into 1 eight-count instead of letting the Vacílala breathe on 1-8 and completing the Dile Que No on 9-16.
variations: Fast 1-eight-count version where the leader sends the follower on 1-3 and immediately catches the next follower into Dile Que No on 5-6-7.
notes: Confirm whether your classes teach the 1-eight-count fast transition (Vacílala on 1-3, Dame on 5-7) or the 2-eight-count standard transition (Vacílala on 1-7, Dame on 9-15).

name: Vacílala y Florea
summary: A stylish, expressive Vacílala variation where both partners embellish ('florean') the open turn with circular Paseo walks, Rumba Guaguancó play, and hand/arm flourishes before reconnecting.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a smooth Vacílala on 1-3, releasing connection to let the follower travel freely.
Circle the follower on 5-6-7 while 'floreando'—adding theatrical Cuban arm framing, cape-like passes, or playful Guaguancó decoys without touching.
Complete the circular orbit on 9-11, present a clear open frame on 12, and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Vacílala turn on 1-2-3 with controlled spotting.
'Florea' (blossom/embellish) on 5-6-7 with sweeping arm styling, skirt work, and circular walks while maintaining eye contact with the leader.
Glide into the pickup frame on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: Turning your back on your partner and ignoring them during the 'floreo' section.
Drifting too far apart so you cannot reach each other cleanly by count 12.
Rushing the arm styling instead of breathing with the music.
variations: Leader drops to one knee or executes a slow body wave while the follower circles.
notes: In Cuban dance slang, 'florear' means to adorn, show off, and play musically with your partner without rushing back into turn patterns.

name: Vacílala y Florea Doble
summary: A showy Rueda figure where the leader leads a Vacílala turn on counts 1-3, then both partners perform two full phrases of expressive solo styling/shines ('florea doble') before reconnecting (or changing partners) in Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Step back on 1 and give a clear Vacílala turn lead on 2-3, releasing the follower to turn solo while you open into your first 'florea' (Rumba/Orisha/Timba solo styling) on 5-6-7.
Continue improvising a second full eight-count of expressive solo styling ('florea doble') on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15), maintaining visual interplay.
On counts 17-24, step in to collect the follower (or the next follower if called with Dame) on 1-2-3 and lead her through Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

followerSteps.text: Execute the clockwise Vacílala turn on 1-2-3 and flow directly into your first 'florea' solo styling phrase (arm styling, hip circularity, or rumba accents) on 5-6-7.
Perform a second full eight-count of solo 'florea' expression on 1-2-3 (counts 9-11) and 5-6-7 (counts 13-15) while staying on your Rueda station.
On counts 17-24, reconnect with the leader's frame on 1-2-3 and travel cleanly across in Dile Que No on 5-6-7.

commonMistakes: Followers wandering off the circle perimeter during the two eight-counts of free styling.
Losing the 1-2-3, 5-6-7 internal pulse while improvising the 'florea' and missing the count 17 pickup.
Leaders grabbing the follower abruptly on count 17 instead of offering a clear visual and frame invitation on counts 15-16.
variations: Vacílala y florea doble con dame (leaders travel to the next partner during the second eight-count of florea).
notes: UNSURE: Confirm whether 'Vacílala y Florea Doble' in your Rueda keeps the same partner at the end or advances to the next partner (add 'partner-change' tag if it advances).

name: Vacílense
summary: The mutual version of Vacílala: both leader and follower execute simultaneous free turns while traveling around their shared circular orbit before reconnecting in Dile Que No or Guapea.

leaderSteps.text: From open Guapea on 1, give a clear inward rotational prep with the left-to-right connection, release on 2, and execute your own clockwise (right) free turn along the circle on 2-3.
Continue traveling forward around the circle on 5-6-7 to pick up the follower in closed or open frame for Dile Que No.

followerSteps.text: Feel the Vacílala prep on 1, release hands, and execute a smooth right (clockwise) traveling turn along the circle on 1-2-3.
Complete the circular walk on 5-6-7, spotting the leader early to reconnect smoothly on count 7.

commonMistakes: Spinning frantically on the spot instead of traveling along the perimeter of the circle on 1-2-3.
Throwing the partner's arm on count 1, which pulls both dancers off balance.
Failing to spot each other on count 3, leading to a clumsy reconnection on 5-7.
variations: Adding a solo clap, shoulder shimmy, or Rumba accent on counts 4-5 before reconnecting.
notes: In Rueda de Casino, 'Vacílense' (or 'Vacílala los dos') means both leaders and followers turn simultaneously without holding hands.

name: Vacílense los Dos
summary: A Rueda and Casino figure where both leader and follower execute simultaneous solo turns on counts 1-3 (mirroring a mutual Vacílala), then reconnect on 5-7 to finish with Dile Que No (or advance to the next partner if called with Dame).

leaderSteps.text: Step back on 1, give a light Vacílala lead on 2 while releasing the hand, and execute your own solo left (or right) turn on 2-3 alongside the follower; step forward on 5-6-7 to collect the follower in closed hold.

If staying with the same partner (or after stabilizing on 9-11), lead the follower cleanly across in a Dile Que No on 5-6-7 (or 1-8 total if done in 1 eight-count; 2 eight-counts if adding a Paseo/Exhibela check).

followerSteps.text: Take the Vacílala prep on 1 and execute a smooth clockwise right turn on 2-3 while the leader turns simultaneously, continuing around the circle arc on 5-6-7.
Reconnect with the leader's frame and complete the Dile Que No exit to return to Guapea.

commonMistakes: Leaders throwing their own turn on count 1 before giving the follower her clear lead, causing the follower to just do a basic.
Both partners drifting apart during the simultaneous turns and missing the reconnection.
Over-rotating and losing visual spotting of the partner.
variations: 1-eight-count social Casino version (simultaneous turns on 1-3, Dile Que No directly on 5-6-7).
Vacílense los dos y dame (leader turns toward the next follower in the Rueda to change partners).
notes: UNSURE: the library already has Vacílense, where both partners turn too. Teachers should say how Vacílense los dos differs, or merge the two. In 1 eight-count, the turns happen on 1-3 and Dile Que No on 5-7. In Rueda, if combined with a Paseo or Dame, it spans 2 eight-counts. Check whether your teachers count this as 1 or 2 eight-counts in the Rueda syllabus.

name: Vamos Abajo / Vamos Arriba
summary: The directional marching calls in closed Rueda position: on 'Vamos Abajo' the leaders walk backward (followers forward) anticlockwise around the ring; on 'Vamos Arriba' the direction reverses so leaders walk forward clockwise.

leaderSteps.text: In closed hold for Vamos Abajo: step left foot back-and-side on 1-2-3 and right foot back on 5-6-7, traveling anticlockwise around the circle while guiding the follower forward.
When 'Vamos Arriba' (or 'Arriba') is called: check direction cleanly on 1-3 and walk forward clockwise around the circle on 5-7 while guiding the follower backward.

followerSteps.text: In closed hold for Vamos Abajo: walk forward anticlockwise around the circle on right (1-2-3) and left (5-6-7), keeping your chest connected to the leader's frame.
When 'Vamos Arriba' is called: feel the leader's chest check on 1-3 and walk backward clockwise around the circle on 5-7.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Leaders taking huge backward steps during Vamos Abajo and stepping on the couple behind them.
Reversing direction abruptly on the wrong foot instead of using the 1-2-3 rock check.
Breaking closed hold into Guapea without a 'Dile Que No' call.
variations: Adding 'Me La Llevo' (continuous fast walking around the circle).
notes: To exit Vamos Abajo / Vamos Arriba back into open Rueda, the caller shouts 'Dile Que No'.

name: Ya Tú Sabes
summary: 'You Already Know!': a signature house/school Rueda combination that chains an Enchufla or Setenta entry with a playful rhythmic break, clap, or body isolation before switching partners into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead an Enchufla or Setenta entry on 1-3 and transition into the signature check/wrap on 5-7.
Hit the '¡Ya tú sabes!' rhythmic break and Cuban attitude pose on 1-3 and 5-7 while advancing toward the next follower.
Collect the new follower on 1-3 and complete Dile Que No on 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Turn cleanly through the 1-3 entry and settle into the check on 5-7.
Match the '¡Ya tú sabes!' rhythmic break, shoulder shimmy, and vocal shout on 1-3 and 5-7.
Connect with the incoming leader on 1-3 and walk through Dile Que No on 5-7.

commonMistakes: Dropping the energy on the vocal/styling break.
Losing the count 17 pickup.
variations: 2-bar compact Ya Tú Sabes.
notes: UNSURE: Because 'Ya tú sabes' is a classic Cuban catchphrase, almost every Rueda school attaches its own signature mini-routine to it. Teacher must verify BOH Studios' exact sequence.

name: Yambú Basics
summary: The oldest, slowest, and most sensual style of Cuban Rumba: couples dance with understated, fluid elegance, playful courtship gestures, and the famous rule 'En el Yambú no se vacuna' (there is no vacunao pelvic thrust in Yambú).

leaderSteps.text: Adopt a relaxed, slightly bent-knee stance (often evoking the gentle, dignified movement of elders) and step a slow, smooth lateral Rumba basic on 1-3 and 5-7 while framing the follower with a handkerchief (pañuelo) or open hands.
Circle the follower gallantly on 1-3 and 5-7; even if an opening appears, never execute a vacunao—instead, offer a respectful bow or suave arm flourish.

followerSteps.text: Glide through slow, grounded lateral Rumba steps on 1-3 and 5-7, using your skirt and shoulders for understated, graceful coquetry without needing to guard against a vacunao.
Turn and play off the leader's courtship framing on 1-3 and 5-7 with soft figure-8 hip motion and warm eye contact.

commonMistakes: Executing an aggressive Guaguancó vacunao pelvic thrust during Yambú (violating the fundamental traditional rule: 'En el Yambú no se vacuna').
Dancing too fast and athletic instead of sinking into Yambú's slow, lyrical cadence.
variations: Incorporating Yambú's slow, gallant courtship feel during lyrical Timba intros.
notes: Key cultural quiz point for students: Yambú, Guaguancó, and Columbia are the three main styles of Cuban Rumba, and Yambú is distinguished by its slower tempo and the absence of the vacunao.

name: Yemayá (Orisha of the Ocean & Universal Motherhood)
summary: Dedicated study of Yemayá, the queen of the ocean and universal mother of the Orishas—transitioning from the calm, maternal rocking of gentle sea swells into powerful, crashing ocean waves and rapid whirlpool spins.

leaderSteps.text: Sway laterally on 1-3 and 5-7 with deep knee flexion and fluid thoracic undulations, sweeping the arms forward and back like rising and falling ocean swells.
As the tempo builds into rough seas, drive powerful torso waves and execute low-to-high 360-degree whirlpool turns ('remolinos') on 1-3 and 5-7.

followerSteps.text: Hold the wide hem of the skirt with both hands on 1-3 and 5-7, lifting and billowing it in smooth figure-8 arcs to emulate whitecaps on the sea while undulating the spine.
Spin dynamically like an ocean whirlpool on 1-3 and whip the skirt upward on 5-7 like a wave crashing over the Malecón.

commonMistakes: Moving only the arms to imitate water while keeping the spine and pelvis rigid; the ocean wave must travel from the knees through the pelvis, ribcage, and shoulders.
Forgetting to breathe through the deep spinal undulations.
variations: Dipping down to scoop the ocean water over your shoulders and head during songs like 'Agua Pa' Yemayá'.
notes: Sacred in Regla de Ocha: Yemayá's colours are ocean blue and crystal/white (alternating in patterns of 7, her sacred number); her attributes include the silver/peacock fan (abanico), seashells, anchor, and half-moon.

name: Yogur
summary: A playful Rueda partner-change figure where an Enchufla on 1-3 brings the couple close together on counts 5-7 for a smooth, grounded pelvic/body-wave groove ('el yogur') before switching partners into Dile Que No.

leaderSteps.text: Lead a standard Enchufla on 1-2-3.
Step close to your current (or next) follower on 5-6-7 with feet wide and knees bent, executing a smooth upward-or-downward body wave and circular hip roll.
Advance to the next follower on 9-11 and lead Dile Que No on 13-15.

followerSteps.text: Execute the Enchufla left turn on 1-2-3.
Mirror the leader's grounded stance on 5-6-7, performing a smooth thoracic ribcage wave and hip isolation without physical weight leaning.
Connect with the incoming leader on 9-11 and walk through Dile Que No on 13-15.

commonMistakes: SAFETY: Invading the partner's personal space too aggressively; keep the body wave playful, respectful, and self-supported.
Bending stiffly at the lower back instead of rolling through the knees and thoracic spine.
variations: Yogur Doble (repeating the wave on two consecutive 4-counts).
notes: Confirm whether BOH Studios performs the Yogur wave with the outgoing partner on 5-7 before moving, or with the incoming partner.
